sources.shows: A two-month art installation in St Peter’s Chapel, Lucerne (2024) placed an AI “Jesus” avatar in a confessional; about 900 conversations took place and many visitors reported feeling inspired, while church leaders were divided.
sources.application: Shows the pull of embodied religious personas, and why the setting adds authority.
sources.limits: An art project with a self-selected audience and the organisers’ own survey.

sources.title: The Translators to the Reader (preface to the 1611 King James Version)
sources.author: Miles Smith for the KJV translators, 1611 · Christian Classics Ethereal Library
sources.shows: The translators defended marginal alternatives, quoting Augustine that “variety of Translations is profitable for the finding out of the sense of the Scriptures”.
sources.application: Offer comparison as a faithful practice, and show where translators themselves weighed alternatives.
sources.limits: A historical preface defending one translation.

sources.title: Translating the Message: The Missionary Impact on Culture
sources.author: Lamin Sanneh · Orbis, 1989 (review)
sources.shows: Argues that translatability is intrinsic to Christianity: entering every vernacular gives each language and culture standing to carry the word of God.
sources.application: Treat translation and language choice as central, not as a settings detail.
sources.limits: A review of a historical and missiological argument.

sources.title: Toward a Science of Translating: formal and dynamic equivalence
sources.author: Eugene Nida, 1964 · excerpt on bible-researcher.com
sources.shows: Nida distinguished formal equivalence (attention to the source form) from dynamic equivalence (attention to the receptor’s response); the latter became the most widely used approach in Bible translation after the Second World War.
sources.application: Explain a translation’s approach in plain words when people choose.
sources.limits: Translation theory; most translations mix both approaches.

sources.title: Review of D. A. Carson, Exegetical Fallacies
sources.author: Wisconsin Lutheran Seminary, reviewing Carson (1984) and James Barr’s The Semantics of Biblical Language (1961)
sources.shows: Barr and Carson warn against word-study fallacies such as the root fallacy: meaning is set by usage in context, not by a word’s etymology or a single gloss.
sources.application: Label interlinear glosses as word aids and show how translations render a word in context.
sources.limits: Scholarly argument summarised in a review.

sources.title: 2025 global Scripture access
sources.author: Wycliffe Global Alliance
sources.shows: As of August 2025 the full Bible is available in 776 languages, the New Testament in 1,798 more, and portions in 1,433 more, of 7,396 languages.
sources.application: Design translation pickers for many languages and partial Bibles, not only English editions.
sources.limits: Organisation’s own statistics.

sources.title: Multiple text integration: a review
sources.author: Liron Primor and Tami Katzir · Frontiers in Psychology, 2018
sources.shows: Building one coherent understanding from several texts on the same subject is a distinct, demanding skill that draws on both word-level and higher-level processes.
sources.application: Comparison is work: help readers connect the texts, for example by marking what differs.
sources.limits: Research on expository texts, not translations of one source.

sources.title: The effects of line length and method of movement on patterns of reading from screen
sources.author: Mary Dyson and Gary Kipping · Visible Language 32(2), 1998
sources.shows: Very short lines (25 characters) were read more slowly than long lines (100 characters), with comprehension unchanged; readers preferred about 55 characters.
sources.application: Side-by-side columns on a phone make very short lines; stack panes instead.
sources.limits: Desktop screens and English prose.

sources.title: Berean Bible terms and conditions
sources.author: Berean Bible
sources.shows: The Berean Standard Bible was dedicated to the public domain on 30 April 2023.
sources.application: Public-domain modern translations can be compared, quoted and shared without licence limits.
sources.limits: Publisher statement.

sources.title: ESV permissions guide
sources.author: Crossway
sources.shows: Up to 500 verses may be quoted without a licence, within limits on proportion of a book and of the work, and not in commentaries or reference works.
sources.application: Licensed translations need agreements for full-text comparison; show only what you are allowed to.
sources.limits: One publisher’s terms; others differ.

sources.title: Understanding Language of Parts
sources.author: W3C WAI · WCAG 2.2 success criterion 3.1.2
sources.shows: Passages in a different language need their language identified so assistive technology can pronounce them.
sources.application: Tag Greek and Hebrew text with its language, and test right-to-left layout.
sources.limits: Accessibility guidance; screen reader support for ancient Greek and Hebrew varies.

sources.title: Annotation: from paper books to the digital library
sources.author: Catherine C. Marshall · ACM Digital Libraries, 1997
sources.shows: A study of annotations in some 410 used university textbooks found placemarks, procedural signals, interpretation and problem working; students sought out well-annotated copies.
sources.application: Support several kinds of mark, from a place to return to a written interpretation, and value others’ notes cautiously.
sources.limits: Textbooks in one university setting; paper, not apps.

sources.title: The Works of Jonathan Edwards, vol. 24: The “Blank Bible”
sources.author: Yale University Press
sources.shows: From 1730 Edwards wrote over five thousand notes in a Bible interleaved with blank pages, over three decades.
sources.application: Reading with a pen is a long devotional and scholarly practice; notes deserve durability and export.
sources.limits: One exceptional reader.

sources.title: Improving students’ learning with effective learning techniques
sources.author: Dunlosky and colleagues · Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 2013 (press summary)
sources.shows: Of ten study techniques, highlighting and underlining were rated low utility; practice testing and distributed practice were rated high.
sources.application: Treat highlighting as a way to return, not as learning; offer notes and recall for those who want to remember.
sources.limits: Educational learning outcomes, not devotional reading.

sources.title: The generation effect: a meta-analytic review
sources.author: Bertsch, Pesta, Wiscott and McDaniel · Memory & Cognition, 2007
sources.shows: Across 86 studies, information people generate themselves is remembered better than information they only read (effect size about 0.40).
sources.application: A note in the reader’s own words does more for memory than a highlight.
sources.limits: Laboratory memory tasks, mostly word lists.

sources.title: Understanding Use of Color
sources.author: W3C WAI · WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.1
sources.shows: Colour must not be the only visual means of conveying information or distinguishing an element.
sources.application: Give each kind of mark a shape or label, and distinguish saved marks from selection and playback without colour.
sources.limits: Accessibility guidance.

sources.title: Spatial contiguity and spatial split-attention effects in multimedia learning environments: a meta-analysis
sources.author: Noah L. Schroeder and Ada T. Cenkci · Educational Psychology Review 30(3), 2018
sources.shows: Learners who had related information placed close together outperformed those who had it separated, on both retention and transfer tests.
sources.application: Keep help near the verse it explains, or keep the verse visible while the help is open.
sources.limits: Learning studies with diagrams and text, not Scripture.

sources.title: Page Previews
sources.author: Wikimedia Foundation · MediaWiki
sources.shows: A/B tests on several Wikipedias found that hover previews let readers check a link without leaving the article: full page views fell, while deliberate interactions with linked pages rose.
sources.application: A short preview anchored to the text lets readers glance at help without losing their place.
sources.limits: Desktop hover previews on an encyclopaedia; touch behaviour differs.

sources.title: The cost of interrupted work: more speed and stress
sources.author: Gloria Mark, Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke · CHI 2008
sources.shows: People interrupted during a task compensated by working faster, at the cost of more stress, frustration, time pressure and effort.
sources.application: Help that takes over the screen is an interruption; make the way back immediate and show where the reader was.
sources.limits: Office email tasks with external interruptions, not self-chosen study.

sources.title: Bottom sheets
sources.author: Google · Material Design 3
sources.shows: Standard bottom sheets sit alongside the main content and let people use both; modal sheets block the content behind a scrim until dismissed.
sources.application: Use a standard sheet when readers should keep reading beside the help, and a modal one only for a focused task.
sources.limits: Platform guidance; does not address Scripture.

sources.title: Bible, glossed: Mark
sources.author: Free Library of Philadelphia · Rare Book Department
sources.shows: Glossed Bibles set Scripture in a central block in a large hand, with short glosses between the lines and longer commentary in the margins in a smaller script; the Glossa Ordinaria became the standard medieval commentary.
sources.application: A long tradition separates Scripture from help by place and type; keep that distinction visible on screen.
sources.limits: One manuscript description; layouts varied.

sources.title: Matthew Henry’s Concise Commentary on Psalm 23
sources.author: Matthew Henry (1706) · public-domain text on Bible Hub
sources.shows: A devotional reading of verse 4: “It is but the shadow of death: the shadow of a serpent will not sting, nor the shadow of a sword kill.”
sources.application: Quoted in the working example with author and date.
sources.limits: One devotional voice from 1706.

sources.title: Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges on Psalm 23:4
sources.author: A. F. Kirkpatrick (1891) · public-domain text on Bible Hub
sources.shows: A philological reading: the Hebrew may be read tsalmûth, “deep gloom”, rather than “shadow of death”.
sources.application: Shows two voices reading one verse differently; quoted in the working example.
sources.limits: Nineteenth-century scholarship; later scholars differ.

sources.title: Understanding Captions (Prerecorded)
sources.author: W3C WAI · WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.2.2
sources.shows: Prerecorded audio in synchronised media needs captions.
sources.application: Caption every sermon clip and video, and correct automatic transcripts before quoting them.
sources.limits: Accessibility guidance.

sources.title: Daily Bread: M’Cheyne’s calendar for daily readings, with his preface
sources.author: Robert Murray M’Cheyne, 1842 · Vernal Presbyterian Church
sources.shows: M’Cheyne named four dangers of his own calendar: formality (“let the calendar perish rather than this rust eat up your souls”), self-righteousness, careless reading and “a yoke too heavy to bear”: “throw aside the fetter, and feed at liberty in the sweet garden of God.”
sources.application: A plan’s own author put the reader’s freedom above the schedule; build that freedom into the plan.
sources.limits: A pastor’s preface, not a study.

sources.title: The Rule of Benedict, chapter 18: the order for reciting the psalms
sources.author: Saint Benedict, 6th century · Saint Meinrad Archabbey translation
sources.shows: After setting out the weekly psalter in detail, Benedict counsels anyone who finds the distribution unsatisfactory “to arrange whatever he judges better”, provided the whole psalter is sung each week.
sources.application: Keep the purpose of a rhythm fixed and let its arrangement change.
sources.limits: A monastic rule for a community, not individual readers.

sources.title: On or off track: how (broken) streaks affect consumer decisions
sources.author: Jackie Silverman and Alixandra Barasch · Journal of Consumer Research 49(6), 2023
sources.shows: In seven studies, highlighting a broken streak reduced later engagement compared with an intact one, regardless of actual behaviour; the effect was stronger when people blamed themselves for the break, and weaker when the streak could be repaired.
sources.application: Counting consecutive days makes a missed day look like a loss; do not make the count the point.
sources.limits: Consumer and lab studies; not Scripture reading.

sources.title: The fresh start effect: temporal landmarks motivate aspirational behavior
sources.author: Hengchen Dai, Katherine L. Milkman and Jason Riis · Management Science, 2014
sources.shows: Goal-directed behaviour (gym visits, “diet” searches, commitments) rises after temporal landmarks such as a new week, month or birthday.
sources.application: A new week or a new day is a natural place to begin again; offer it.
sources.limits: Archival field data on health and goals.

sources.title: Moral emotions and moral behavior
sources.author: June Price Tangney, Jeff Stuewig and Debra J. Mashek · Annual Review of Psychology 58, 2007
sources.shows: Shame, a painful focus on the self, tends to prompt hiding, denial and withdrawal; guilt about a specific act tends to prompt repair.
sources.application: Copy that makes people feel they have failed as readers invites them to stay away.
sources.limits: General moral-emotion research, not app design.

sources.title: The Rule of Benedict, chapter 20: reverence at prayer
sources.author: Saint Benedict, 6th century · Saint Meinrad Archabbey translation
sources.shows: “We are heard not for our many words but for our purity of heart and tears of compunction”; prayer “ought to be short and pure”, and in community “always be short”.
sources.application: Prayer is not measured by length or volume; do not count minutes, and keep shared prayer short and unhurried.
sources.limits: A monastic rule for a community.

sources.title: An Order for Compline
sources.author: Book of Common Prayer (1979) · Episcopal Church · bcponline.org
sources.shows: Night prayer with Officiant and People parts, italic rubrics such as “Silence may be kept”, a confession, short readings, the “Keep watch, dear Lord” prayer and the antiphon “Guide us waking, O Lord”.
sources.application: Quoted in the working example; shows the three kinds of text an office needs to distinguish: rubrics, the leader’s lines and the people’s responses.
sources.limits: One tradition’s office; other churches order night prayer differently.

sources.title: Collects: Season after Pentecost (contemporary)
sources.author: Book of Common Prayer (1979) · Episcopal Church · bcponline.org
sources.shows: Proper 25, the Sunday closest to 26 October, has the collect “Almighty and everlasting God, increase in us the gifts of faith, hope, and charity”.
sources.application: A calendar ties each day to its texts; looking ahead to Sunday shows its collect without changing today.
sources.limits: One church’s calendar.

sources.title: How can I pray? The Daily Examen
sources.author: IgnatianSpirituality.com · Loyola Press
sources.shows: Five steps proposed after Ignatius of Loyola: become aware of God’s presence; review the day with gratitude; pay attention to your emotions; choose one feature of the day and pray from it; look toward tomorrow.
sources.application: A guided outline with a known source; the working example’s prompts are written for it.
sources.limits: A modern adaptation; Ignatius’s own five points in the Spiritual Exercises differ in wording.

sources.title: Poloma and Pendleton’s (1989) Prayer Types Scale in Christian, Jewish, and Muslim praying adults
sources.author: Black, Pössel, Jeppsen, Tariq and Rosmarin · Psychology of Religion and Spirituality 7(3), 2015
sources.shows: Builds on a four-type typology of private prayer (colloquial, meditative, petitionary and ritual); the scale held only partly across Christians, Jews and Muslims, and associations with mental health differed between groups.
sources.application: People pray in distinct ways; one surface will not serve them all, and no single “prayer feature” is neutral.
sources.limits: Self-report survey; correlations, not effects of apps.

sources.title: The hidden cost of personal quantification
sources.author: Jordan Etkin · Journal of Consumer Research 42(6), 2016
sources.shows: In six experiments, measuring an activity (walking, reading) increased how much people did but reduced how much they enjoyed it, by undermining intrinsic motivation.
sources.application: Counting minutes or prayers may raise activity while turning prayer into output; do not measure it.
sources.limits: Leisure activities in experiments, not prayer.

sources.title: Top mental health and prayer apps fail spectacularly at privacy, security
sources.author: Mozilla Foundation · *Privacy Not Included, 2 May 2022
sources.shows: 28 of 32 mental health and prayer apps received the *Privacy Not Included warning; Pray.com was among the worst for sharing personal information with third parties.
sources.application: Prayer data is intimate; keep requests on the device by default and share nothing with advertisers.
sources.limits: A 2022 review; apps’ practices may have changed since.

sources.title: Pray As You Go privacy policy
sources.author: Jesuits in Britain · Pray As You Go
sources.shows: Opens: “We believe prayer is between you and God”, quotes Ignatius’s Spiritual Exercises (15), and states that Pray As You Go does not collect any personal data for users of its app and website.
sources.application: A precedent for making privacy part of a prayer app’s theology, not only its compliance.
sources.limits: The same policy says anonymous navigation and error data may be stored by Google Firebase.

sources.title: The FaithTech Playbook 2.0: Creating Technology Redemptively
sources.author: FaithTech Team · first published 2023, revised 2026
sources.shows: Three postures, reckless (“Move Fast, Break Things”), responsible (“Slow Down, Fix Things”) and redemptive (“Sacrifice, Create Things”), judged by power, person and purpose; three spiritual currents, the Magic Machine Myth, the Limitless Self and the Killer App Trap; four practices, Lament, Discern, Build and Steward.
sources.application: The closest parallel to Praxis’s frame for technology, and the source of the questions about worship and about whether to build at all.
sources.limits: Covers all technology, not faith apps specifically; a community’s framework, not research.

sources.title: Recommend an app to faith.tools: selection criteria
sources.author: Cameron Pak · faith.tools, updated 16 August 2026
sources.shows: Eleven questions for listing an app, including whether it is “beneficial to a Christian’s walk with God and community”, whether costs are “very clear”, whether it aligns “with the teachings in the Bible”, and whether it “properly cite[s] and license[s] the Bible translations it uses”.
sources.application: A curator’s test from the faith-app community itself, close to several of the ten.
sources.limits: One curator’s criteria for a directory; not a design framework.

sources.title: 6 Guardrails for AI Apps for Christians
sources.author: Cam Pak · faith.tools, updated 24 July 2026
sources.shows: AI output must be biblically accurate, must not fabricate or misrepresent Scripture, “must clearly identify as AI, not human”, “must not replace human relationships or spiritual practices” (“Can AI truly pray for you? No, it’s artificial.”), must balance grace and truth, and must not invent personal facts.
sources.application: The clearest statement from within the faith-app community of what “Never speak for God” rules out for AI.
sources.limits: Unofficial rules for one directory’s listings.

sources.title: What is redemptive entrepreneurship?
sources.author: Praxis
sources.shows: Sets out three ways to build: Exploitative (“take all you can get”, “I win, you lose”), Ethical (“do things right … do no harm, keep the rules, play fair”, “I win, you win”) and Redemptive (“creative restoration through sacrifice”, “I sacrifice, we win”), across strategy, operations and leadership.
sources.application: The frame used on every deep dive to ask what each design choice takes, keeps or gives.
sources.limits: Written for founders and businesses, not specifically for interface design.

sources.title: Familiar yet strange: why we call our work “redemptive”
sources.author: Scott Kauffmann, Andy Crouch and RuthAnn Deveney · Praxis, 2023, republished 31 August 2026
sources.shows: Explains the choice of the word: Christ’s pattern of “creative restoration through sacrifice” as a model for vocation, and God’s invitation to “participate with him in the restoration of all things”; acknowledges that explicitly theological language can feel exclusive and argues the word works as invitation.
sources.application: Grounds the frame in participation in God’s work rather than in human achievement.
sources.limits: An organisation explaining its own vocabulary.

sources.title: The Redemptive Business playbook: products
sources.author: Praxis
sources.shows: Redemptive products “genuinely benefit our customers, their communities, and the world” while minimising downsides; aim for “impact/market fit, not merely product/market fit”, and make “what people want to want”.
sources.application: Close to this reference’s question for every option: what good does this serve, and for whom?
sources.limits: A business playbook; not specific to faith apps or interfaces.

sources.title: Code of Canon Law, canons 822–833: instruments of social communication and books
sources.author: Holy See · Code of Canon Law (1983)
sources.shows: Canon 825 §1: books of the sacred Scriptures “cannot be published unless the Apostolic See or the conference of bishops has approved them”; §2 allows translations prepared with other Christians, “provided with appropriate annotations”.
sources.application: Shows that for Catholic readers, which edition and which notes is a matter of church approval, not only preference.
sources.limits: Applies to the Catholic Church.

sources.title: Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation, Dei Verbum
sources.author: Second Vatican Council · 18 November 1965
sources.shows: §22: “Easy access to Sacred Scripture should be provided for all the Christian faithful.” §25: prayer should accompany reading “so that God and man may talk together”; editions “provided with suitable footnotes” should be prepared also for non-Christians.
sources.application: Access, help and prayer belong together in Catholic teaching on Scripture.
sources.limits: Catholic magisterial teaching.

sources.title: On Christian Doctrine, Book I
sources.author: Augustine of Hippo · c. 397 · New Advent translation
sources.shows: “Whoever, then, thinks that he understands the Holy Scriptures … but puts such an interpretation upon them as does not tend to build up this twofold love of God and our neighbor, does not yet understand them as he ought.”
sources.application: A test for notes, answers and interpretations: do they build up love?
sources.limits: Augustine’s hermeneutic, one classical voice among many.

sources.title: Luthers Übersetzungsmethode (on the Sendbrief vom Dolmetschen, 1530)
sources.author: Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft
sources.shows: Luther urged translators to ask the mother at home, the children in the street and the common man in the market, and to listen to how they speak.
sources.application: Translation and interface language serve ordinary readers.
sources.limits: One translator’s method; formal-equivalence traditions weigh it differently.

sources.title: Life Together (review)
sources.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer, 1939 · 9Marks review
sources.shows: Written from the Finkenwalde seminary; balances “The Day with Others” (Scripture, song and prayer together) with “The Day Alone” (solitude, silence, meditation), and ends with confession and communion.
sources.application: Holds personal and communal practice together.
sources.limits: Read through a review; quotations are not taken from the text here.

sources.title: The Use of Money (Sermon 50)
sources.author: John Wesley · Wesley Center Online, 1872 edition
sources.shows: Three rules: “Gain all you can”, “save all you can”, “give all you can”. Gain is limited by love of neighbour: “This is dear-bought gain. And so is whatever is procured by hurting our neighbour in his soul”.
sources.application: Earning from honest work is not suspect in itself; what matters is whether it harms the person served, and what is done with the gain.
sources.limits: An eighteenth-century sermon on trade and work, not on ministry or apps.

sources.title: The Small Catechism
sources.author: Martin Luther · Book of Concord
sources.shows: Each part is headed “As the head of the family should teach them in a simple way to his household”, followed by questions such as “What does this mean?”
sources.application: Teaching the faith to children was given to households first, with short questions and plain answers.
sources.limits: A Lutheran confessional text; other traditions teach children differently.

sources.title: The Life We’re Looking For: Reclaiming Relationship in a Technological World
sources.author: Andy Crouch · Convergent, 2022
sources.shows: Argues that persons are made for recognition and love, and that technology’s promise of effortless “superpowers” costs us our humanness.
sources.application: A Christian account of personhood against which to judge companion-like and effortless features.
sources.limits: Read through publisher material and reviews.

sources.title: You Are What You Love: The Spiritual Power of Habit
sources.author: James K. A. Smith · Brazos, 2016
sources.shows: Argues that we are formed by what we love, and that habits act as “liturgies”, including “secular liturgies” loaded with a story about who we are.
sources.application: Streaks, badges and feeds are habits that form desire; design them as liturgies.
sources.limits: Read through listings and reviews.

sources.title: Eat This Book: A Conversation in the Art of Spiritual Reading
sources.author: Eugene H. Peterson · Eerdmans, 2006
sources.shows: Commends lectio divina and slow, participatory reading of Scripture, and discusses translation from his work on The Message.
sources.application: Supports designs for slow reading and keeping.
sources.limits: Read through the listing.

sources.title: Albert Borgmann (Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.author: On Technology and the Character of Contemporary Life · University of Chicago Press, 1984
sources.shows: Contrasts the “device paradigm”, which delivers commodities effortlessly, with “focal things and practices” that require attention, engagement and skill; argues technology should support rather than supplant them.
sources.application: A frame for asking whether an app supports the practice of reading and prayer or replaces it.
sources.limits: Philosophy of technology, not theology, though Borgmann wrote as a Catholic.

sources.title: The Way of the Heart: Desert Spirituality and Contemporary Ministry
sources.author: Henri J. M. Nouwen · 1981 · Henri Nouwen Society
sources.shows: Draws on the desert fathers and mothers of the fourth and fifth centuries to commend three disciplines, solitude, silence and prayer, as a way out of noise and busyness into a life centred in God.
sources.application: Grounds quiet prayer and silence in a long tradition.
sources.limits: Read through the book page; no quotation used.

sources.title: Parasocial intimacy, change, and nostalgia in podcast listener reviews
sources.author: M. Olguta Vilceanu · Media and Communication 13, 2025
sources.shows: A semantic network analysis of over 12,000 podcast reviews found hosts and content central to the trust-based connections listeners form, with nostalgia and attachment showing when hosts or formats change.
sources.application: Hosts become trusted, friend-like voices; name them honestly, and do not let a host’s voice stand in for Scripture or for a pastor.
sources.limits: Reviews of general podcasts, not faith audio.

sources.title: Listening to music for insomnia in adults
sources.author: Jespersen et al. · Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2022
sources.shows: 13 trials, 1,007 participants: listening to sedative or relaxing music may improve sleep quality (moderate-certainty evidence); evidence on insomnia severity is very uncertain.
sources.application: Sleep audio can genuinely help; design it to fade into silence rather than to keep someone listening.
sources.limits: Music, not spoken or Scripture content.

sources.title: How the design of YouTube influences user sense of agency
sources.author: Kai Lukoff et al. · CHI 2021
sources.shows: In a survey of 120 users, autoplay and recommendations mainly undermined people’s sense of agency, while search and playlists supported it; co-design participants with a specific intention preferred designs that gave them more agency.
sources.application: End sessions and let listeners choose what comes next; do not autoplay.
sources.limits: Video, not devotional audio.

sources.title: Rules of the Band-Societies
sources.author: John Wesley, 25 December 1738 · Holy Joys transcription
sources.shows: The design of the meetings is “to obey that command of God, ‘Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed’”; four questions are asked at every meeting, beginning “What known sins have you committed since our last meeting?”
sources.application: Regular self-examination with set questions is an old Christian practice, and it happened among people who knew and prayed for each other, not on a chart.
sources.limits: A small-group discipline for committed members, not a public survey.

sources.title: Natural Church Development Survey
sources.author: Free Methodist Church in Canada · NCD Canada
sources.shows: The survey is “completed by 30 people from the congregation chosen according to specific criteria”, measures eight “Quality Characteristics” of church life, and lets leaders “identify the church’s most critical health issues” and track trends over repeated surveys.
sources.application: A church assessment can be anonymous and aggregated, and its result can start a conversation about where to focus.
sources.limits: A denomination’s description of the tool, not an evaluation of it.

sources.title: Book review: Natural Church Development by Christian Schwarz
sources.author: John Ellas and Flavil Yeakley · Journal of the American Society for Church Growth 10(2), 1999
sources.shows: Two church-growth researchers welcome the book’s pastoral reach but criticise the research behind its claims, which they call “pseudo-science”.
sources.application: Be modest about what a church score shows; a survey of perceptions is not a measure of health or faithfulness.
sources.limits: A review, from within the church-growth movement.

sources.title: Network: discover your spiritual gifts, personal style and passion
sources.author: Bruce L. Bugbee and Don Cousins · Zondervan, developed with the Willow Creek Association
sources.shows: Invites participants to “discover your spiritual gifts, personal style, and God-given passion for serving in the body of Christ”; the course pairs self-assessment with consultants who help people find a place to serve.
sources.application: Gifts assessment has long been tied to serving and to a conversation with another person, not just a result screen.
sources.limits: A publisher’s description.

sources.title: Relationships between personality and spiritual gifts
sources.author: Kenneth J. Stone · Doctor of Psychology dissertation, George Fox University, 1991
sources.shows: Compared a spiritual gifts inventory with a five-factor personality measure among church members: personality accounted for about 50% of the shared variance, and Openness and Extraversion correlated with two of three gift factors; the author recommends reconsidering reliance on gift inventories.
sources.application: Present inventory results as what someone enjoys and how they see themselves, and point to serving and to other people for confirmation.
sources.limits: One inventory and one sample.

sources.title: Am I growing yet?
sources.author: Mark Galli · Christianity Today, 25 October 2007
sources.shows: Reports on Willow Creek’s Reveal survey, which found that mature believers felt they were “not being fed”, and on the church’s plan to coach “self-feeders” with personal growth plans; Galli asks whether constant self-monitoring of growth serves discipleship.
sources.application: Even careful spiritual measurement raises a theological question: what does tracking one’s own growth do to a person who is meant to look outward?
sources.limits: Commentary on a church’s survey, not a study of apps.

sources.title: Putting feelings into words: affect labeling disrupts amygdala activity in response to affective stimuli
sources.author: Matthew D. Lieberman et al. · Psychological Science 18(5), 2007
sources.shows: Labelling the emotion in a picture reduced amygdala response to negative images compared with other ways of processing them, with increased right ventrolateral prefrontal activity.
sources.application: Naming a feeling may help in itself; a check-in can end at the naming, without a score or a chart.
sources.limits: Laboratory study with images, not mood apps.

sources.title: Ecological momentary assessment
sources.author: Saul Shiffman, Arthur A. Stone and Michael R. Hufford · Annual Review of Clinical Psychology 4, 2008
sources.shows: Repeatedly sampling people’s current experience in daily life reduces recall bias and reveals patterns, and is used in research and clinical care.
sources.application: Daily check-ins are a recognised method; outside research and care, decide who benefits from the record and how long it should exist.
sources.limits: A method review for researchers and clinicians.

sources.title: The fallacy of personal validation: a classroom demonstration of gullibility
sources.author: Bertram R. Forer · Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology 44(1), 1949
sources.shows: Students rated an identical, generic personality sketch as highly accurate for themselves.
sources.application: Personal-sounding reports feel true whatever their basis; say how a result was produced and what it cannot claim.
sources.limits: A classroom demonstration; later studies refined it.

sources.title: What the Christian app Soultime has discovered with its mood tracker
sources.author: Hope 103.2 · 12 May 2020
sources.shows: Soultime described lockdown mood trends across its users and said: “We don’t track people individually, as privacy is very important”.
sources.application: A precedent for using check-ins only in aggregate; say so in the app, and show where individual records are kept.
sources.limits: A news interview; data practices were not independently verified.

sources.title: HelloBible: interactive Bible (App Store listing)
sources.author: HelloBox · Apple App Store
sources.shows: Describes an experience “tailored to your reality and pace” for students, young adults, parents, people in doubt, Catholics, Protestants, Evangelicals and people without religious affiliation; the privacy label lists contact information and identifiers linked to the user for analytics and personalisation.
sources.application: Personalisation by life situation and church is common; say what each answer changes and what is linked to the person.
sources.limits: A store listing; the onboarding itself was not tested here.

sources.title: Evaluating verifiability in generative search engines
sources.author: Nelson F. Liu, Tianyi Zhang and Percy Liang · Findings of EMNLP 2023
sources.shows: Audited answers from four generative search engines: “a mere 51.5% of generated sentences are fully supported by citations and only 74.5% of citations support their associated sentence.”
sources.application: A citation marker is a claim that needs checking, not proof; put the cited words where people can compare them.
sources.limits: General web search engines in 2023, not Bible assistants; systems have changed since.

sources.title: Citations and trust in LLM generated responses
sources.author: Yifan Ding et al. · AAAI 2025
sources.shows: Trust rose when answers carried citations, and this “held true even when the citations were random”; trust fell when participants checked the citations.
sources.application: Citations persuade whether or not they support the claim. Make checking easy, and make sure what is cited says what the answer says.
sources.limits: An online experiment with general questions; effects in religious study may differ.

sources.title: Icon usability
sources.author: Aurora Harley · Nielsen Norman Group · 2014
sources.shows: Few icons are universally recognised; “Icon labels should be visible at all times”, and hover-only labels fail on touch screens.
sources.application: A row of unlabelled icons under an answer asks people to guess; label them, or keep two or three and put the rest in a labelled menu.
sources.limits: Practitioner guidance from usability testing, not a controlled study.

sources.title: Memory recognition and recall in user interfaces
sources.author: Raluca Budiu · Nielsen Norman Group · 2024
sources.shows: “Recognition is easier than recall because it involves more cues”: interfaces that show options ask less of memory than ones that require people to remember and type.
sources.application: Browsing books and chapters asks people to recognise; a reference field asks them to recall. Offer both.
sources.limits: Practitioner guidance drawing on memory research.

sources.title: Understanding SC 3.3.3: Error Suggestion
sources.author: W3C · WCAG 2.2
sources.shows: When an input error is detected and suggestions are known, suggest a correction to the user.
sources.application: A reference field should say “Did you mean John 3?” rather than “Not found”, and accept common abbreviations.
sources.limits: A conformance criterion, not a usability study.

sources.title: Understanding SC 2.5.8: Target Size (Minimum)
sources.author: W3C · WCAG 2.2
sources.shows: Pointer targets should be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or spaced so that a 24-pixel circle around each does not overlap another.
sources.application: Chapter grids with 150 Psalms and verse grids pack many small targets; size and space them for thumbs.
sources.limits: A minimum, not a recommendation; larger targets help more people.

sources.title: How to pray for intentions on Hallow
sources.author: Hallow help centre
sources.shows: Requests are limited to 240 characters, go to friends, a church or groups, can’t be submitted anonymously or edited, and can be kept private, when they are “only saved to your journal and not shared with others”; others respond with a heart.
sources.application: Show the audience, length limit, anonymity and editing rules before someone writes.
sources.limits: The publisher describing its own feature; it does not say whether parish administrators can read requests.

sources.title: Overview of the Church tab
sources.author: Hallow help centre
sources.shows: Requests can be posted to friends or a church; “Intentions will remain active for 7 days.”
sources.application: An end date by default keeps old needs from lingering in a feed.
sources.limits: Publisher documentation.

sources.title: Expand your care through confidential member groups
sources.author: Jon Aleixo · Planning Center blog · 28 February 2025
sources.shows: Confidential groups hide members from each other, so that “only group leaders will have access to the complete member list”; chat is turned off. The reason given: “Recovery and support groups thrive when participants feel safe enough to attend before eventually opening up.”
sources.application: Support groups can protect members from each other while a named leader stays reachable.
sources.limits: A vendor announcing its own feature; administrators can still see members.

sources.title: YouVersion Prayer
sources.author: YouVersion · bible.com
sources.shows: “Keep your prayers private, or invite friends to pray with you.”
sources.application: Private by default, friends by invitation, is the familiar shape for personal requests.
sources.limits: Marketing copy; no help article found on who sees a shared prayer.

sources.title: Clergy juggle prayer requests with privacy rights
sources.author: Amy Green · United Methodist News Service, 2004 · Baltimore-Washington Conference archive
sources.shows: After complaints about disclosed information, a church suspended printed prayer requests and then asked for “written approval if the prayer is for someone other than themselves”; a lawyer quoted: “There’s really nothing wrong with getting consent for these kinds of disclosures even when you aren’t legally required to do so.”
sources.application: Ask before naming anyone else, even where the law does not require it.
sources.limits: US practice from 2004, before apps; HIPAA does not bind most congregations.

sources.title: Richtlinie der EKD zum Schutz vor sexualisierter Gewalt (Gewaltschutzrichtlinie)
sources.author: Evangelische Kirche in Deutschland · 18 October 2019, amended 24 June 2022 · as published by the Evangelische Landeskirche in Württemberg
sources.shows: Church workers, including volunteers, must report a justified suspicion of sexualised violence without delay to the Melde- und Ansprechstelle (§8), with the confidentiality of their identity protected; pastoral confidentiality and the seal of confession remain untouched. The Melde- und Ansprechstelle is “dem Schutz Betroffener verpflichtet” (§7).
sources.application: A volunteer group leader may not be able to keep a disclosure to themselves; say so before someone shares.
sources.limits: Each Landeskirche implements the guideline in its own law, with different numbering; the EKD planned a revision in 2024. Not a statement of state law.

sources.title: Rahmenordnung Prävention gegen sexualisierte Gewalt
sources.author: Deutsche Bischofskonferenz · in force from 1 January 2020 · as published by the Diocese of Hildesheim
sources.shows: Each institution describes how suspicions and complaints are handled, including internal and external advice and reporting routes, which “müssen in geeigneter Weise bekannt gemacht werden”; for every institution “muss eine für Präventionsfragen geschulte Person zur Verfügung stehen”.
sources.application: An app set up for a Catholic parish or institution can show its trained contact and its reporting routes.
sources.limits: A framework; dioceses set the details in their own Präventionsordnungen, and names for the role differ.

sources.title: Parish Safeguarding Officer toolkit
sources.author: Diocese of Durham, Church of England · November 2023
sources.shows: With the incumbent, the PCC must appoint at least one Parish Safeguarding Officer, who should be a lay person, and make sure the officer’s contact details are displayed in all church premises.
sources.application: Name the safeguarding officer in an app as a church would on its noticeboard.
sources.limits: One diocese’s toolkit applying national Church of England guidance.

sources.title: Zentrale Anlaufstelle.help
sources.author: Run for the EKD and Diakonie by the independent specialist service of Pfiffigunde Heilbronn e.V.
sources.shows: Free advice that is “unabhängig, anonym und unterliegt der Schweigepflicht”; on request it connects people with church and Diakonie contact points, and also informs them about independent alternatives. Phone 0800 5040112.
sources.application: An independent route beside a church’s own contact, for people who will not or cannot go to the church first.
sources.limits: For abuse in Protestant churches and Diakonie in Germany; phone appointments are arranged at set hours.

sources.title: Confidentiality policy
sources.author: thirtyone:eight
sources.shows: Personal information “will not be shared outside Thirtyone:eight without explicit and informed consent”, except where someone is at serious and immediate risk, discloses involvement in abuse, or the law requires it.
sources.application: Say what an independent service does with what it hears, including its limits.
sources.limits: A UK charity’s policy; other services set different limits.

sources.title: Study finds agencies can react more supportively than family and friends to victims’ disclosures of sexual assault
sources.author: National Institute of Justice · 30 October 2018 · on research led by Anne P. DePrince
sources.shows: Among 228 women, “victims reported receiving more negative reactions from informal supports (e.g., peers, family members) than they experienced when disclosing sexual assault to police or community-based service providers”, and informal supports gave less tangible aid and helpful information.
sources.application: Friends and groups are not automatically the safest listeners for something hard; offer someone trained beside them.
sources.limits: A US study of women disclosing sexual assault; not about churches or apps.

sources.title: Small group participation linked to higher discipleship scores
sources.author: Aaron Earls · Lifeway Research · 4 August 2026
sources.shows: US Protestant churchgoers attending a small group five times or more a month scored 74.1 on a discipleship assessment, against 60.4 for those who do not attend one.
sources.application: Groups matter to many people’s faith; design them with care rather than avoid them.
sources.limits: A correlation from self-report; it does not show that groups cause growth. US Protestants only.

sources.title: iOS: Plan with Friends
sources.author: YouVersion Support
sources.shows: “When friends join you in a Plan, you see each other’s progress as you finish days. You can talk about each day’s content in a private discussion area.” Up to 300 friends can be invited; “Only the host of the plan can invite others”; the start date can’t be changed once the plan has started; and “if someone leaves a Plan, they cannot rejoin it.”
sources.application: Show participants what the others will see, and give a way back to someone who left or fell behind.
sources.limits: Publisher documentation for iOS; the interface was not tested end to end.

sources.title: iOS: Plan Privacy
sources.author: YouVersion Support
sources.shows: With Friends Only, “your Plan activity (such as completing Plan Days) will be visible to your friends in their Community Feed”; Plan with Friends activity is visible only to participants; “Plan activities on the Community Feed or your timeline cannot be deleted.”
sources.application: Say where each kind of activity appears before it does, and let people delete it.
sources.limits: Publisher documentation; the default setting is not stated.

sources.title: iOS: Plan with Friends – Comments
sources.author: YouVersion Support
sources.shows: Each day’s comments sit under “Talk It Over”; others can like a comment with a heart, and a reply to an email notification “becomes part of the day’s comment”. Options on a comment “may include Copy, Edit, and Delete”.
sources.application: A discussion per day gives friends somewhere to talk; say who can step in when a comment hurts someone.
sources.limits: The article does not describe reporting or moderation; it may exist elsewhere in the app.

sources.title: Announcing Plans with Friends
sources.author: YouVersion blog · November 2017
sources.shows: “Plans with Friends brings together the best of both”: friends’ perspective “often helps us see things in God’s Word that we might not have noticed on our own”, and “You’ll see one another’s progress as you complete days”.
sources.application: The reason to read together is the conversation; the progress view came with it.
sources.limits: A launch announcement; it gives reasons, not completion figures.

sources.title: A brief history of the Moravian Daily Texts
sources.author: Moravian Church in North America · July 2018
sources.shows: “The first printed edition of the Daily Texts (Losungen) was published in Herrnhut, Saxony, in 1731”; since 1788 the watchwords “have been drawn by lot from a collection of around 2,000 suitable Old Testament texts”, while the doctrinal texts are selected.
sources.application: Christians have read the same words on the same day for centuries without anyone counting who read.
sources.limits: A church’s own history of its publication.

sources.title: Anleitung Bibelteilen
sources.author: Erzbistum Köln · 2020
sources.shows: The seven steps of Bible sharing (the Lumko method); in step 5, “Jede/r spricht von sich in der ersten Person. Keine Diskussion, kein Vortrag.”
sources.application: Give the conversation a shape: each person says what touched them, and nobody corrects anyone.
sources.limits: One diocese’s leaflet; other versions have six steps or name them differently.

sources.title: Methoden praktischer Bibelarbeit
sources.author: Diözese Linz · Bibelwerk
sources.shows: Readers mark verses with a question mark, an exclamation mark (or candle) and an arrow; everyone is invited to bring questions, insights and experiences, and experiences “Ohne Zwang”. Its risks: some verses stay unclear, and “das Problem der ‚Dauerredner‘”.
sources.application: Prompts that invite rather than demand, and a leader who keeps space for quieter voices.
sources.limits: A practical guide, not a study of outcomes.

sources.title: Video calling: safeguarding questions
sources.author: Church of England National Safeguarding Team · April 2020
sources.shows: “We strongly recommend reserving video calling for group chats rather than making one-to-one video calls”, applying the guidance Safer Environment and Activities to the online world.
sources.application: With under-18s, keep contact in the group, not one to one.
sources.limits: Written for video calls during the pandemic; the principle comes from wider guidance.

sources.title: Guidance on use of social media and private messaging with young and vulnerable people
sources.author: All Saints Boyne Hill, Church of England parish · 2026
sources.shows: “Do not use social visual media for one-to-one conversations with young people - use only within group conversations where a minimum of two DBS checked adults are present.”
sources.application: A group app for under-18s can make two leaders the minimum in any conversation.
sources.limits: One parish’s policy applying diocesan guidance; German churches set their own rules.

sources.title: Social comparison features in physical activity promotion apps: scoping meta-review
sources.author: Danielle Arigo, Megan M. Brown, Kristen Pasko and Jerry Suls · Journal of Medical Internet Research, 2020
sources.shows: Improvements from comparison features are “inconsistent”; social comparison “may motivate PA for some people under some circumstances”, and no evidence was found that apps account for people’s “differing preferences for and responses to social comparison information”.
sources.application: Showing everyone’s progress helps some readers and discourages others; let people choose what they see and show.
sources.limits: A review of reviews about physical activity apps, not Bible reading.

sources.title: App Store Review Guidelines
sources.author: Apple
sources.shows: “If your app doesn’t include significant account-based features, let people use it without a login. If your app supports account creation, you must also offer account deletion within the app.” Apps “may not require users to enter personal information to function, except when directly relevant to the core functionality of the app or required by law.”
sources.application: Let people read, pray or ask before they sign up, and let them delete the account they make.
sources.limits: Platform rules for the App Store; enforcement varies, and Google Play has its own rules.

sources.title: Human Interface Guidelines: Onboarding
sources.author: Apple
sources.shows: Onboarding should be “fast, fun, and optional”; “Postpone nonessential setup flows or customization steps”; “Prefer letting people experience your app or game before prompting them for ratings or purchases.”
sources.application: Open on the content; ask for ratings and payment after people have used the app.
sources.limits: Design guidance, not research.

sources.title: Request runtime permissions
sources.author: Android Developers
sources.shows: “Ask for a permission in context, when the user starts to interact with the feature that requires it. Don’t block the user.”
sources.application: Ask for notifications when someone sets a reminder, not at launch.
sources.limits: Platform guidance for Android; Apple’s is similar.

sources.title: Mobile-App Onboarding: An Analysis of Components and Techniques
sources.author: Alita Kendrick · Nielsen Norman Group · 21 June 2020
sources.shows: “Skip Onboarding Whenever Possible”; their research on deck-of-cards tutorials “showed that tutorials didn’t improve task performance”; “lengthy promotional onboarding will likely be skipped.”
sources.application: Spend the effort on a clear first screen rather than slides about it.
sources.limits: An expert article drawing on the group’s own studies; details of those studies are in separate reports.

sources.title: Onboarding Tutorials vs. Contextual Help
sources.author: Nielsen Norman Group
sources.shows: Tutorials are “dramatically overused”, and “we find that users frequently skip them”; “Users want to start using the product right away.”
sources.application: Teach a feature when someone reaches it, not before the first use.
sources.limits: An expert article; the group notes tutorials can help with genuinely new interactions.

sources.title: Guidelines 03/2022 on deceptive design patterns in social media platform interfaces
sources.author: European Data Protection Board · version 2.0, 14 February 2023
sources.shows: “Continuous prompting” occurs “when users are pushed to provide more personal data than necessary for the purposes of processing or to agree with another use of their data, by being repeatedly asked”; at sign-up, users “should understand what exactly they sign up for”.
sources.application: Ask once, for what is needed, and say plainly what someone is signing up for.
sources.limits: Written for social media platforms; it applies the GDPR, which binds other apps too.

sources.title: Cart abandonment rate statistics
sources.author: Baymard Institute
sources.shows: Among US online shoppers who abandoned a checkout for reasons other than “just browsing”, 18% gave the reason “The site wanted me to create an account”.
sources.application: A required account turns some people away at the moment they were ready.
sources.limits: Online shopping, not faith apps; a survey of stated reasons.

sources.title: Start with the Bible
sources.author: Diocese of York (Church of England)
sources.shows: For someone who has “Picked up a Bible and wondering where to begin”: try Mark; “Start with chapter 1 and read as much as feels manageable. You could also listen to it.” It suggests a short prayer before beginning.
sources.application: A church’s first step asks nothing of the reader: a place to start, and permission to read only a little.
sources.limits: One diocese’s page for newcomers.

sources.title: Help from the Bible
sources.author: The Gideons International in Australia
sources.shows: “The front section of all Gideon Bibles and Testaments contains Helps to read the Bible. There are a number of topical indexes to point the reader to what the Bible says about various topics, problems and life situations.”
sources.application: A first page of situations is an old way into Scripture for someone without a reference.
sources.limits: One national association’s description; editions differ.

sources.title: St. Benedict’s Rule for Monasteries
sources.author: Benedict of Nursia, sixth century · Project Gutenberg edition
sources.shows: Chapter 53: “Let all guests who arrive be received like Christ.” Chapter 58, on someone asking to join the community: “let him not be granted an easy entrance”.
sources.application: Welcome guests freely; ask for commitment later, from those who want to stay.
sources.limits: A monastic rule; an app is not a monastery, and the analogy is ours.

sources.title: Code of Canon Law, canons 879–958: the Most Holy Eucharist
sources.author: Holy See
sources.shows: A priest “is permitted to receive an offering to apply the Mass for a specific intention” (can. 945); those who give it “share its concern to support its ministers and works” (can. 946); and “Any appearance of … trading is to be excluded entirely from the offering for Masses” (can. 947).
sources.application: The church has long let people give for the ministry of the word and sacrament, and drawn a line against trading in it.
sources.limits: Catholic church law; Protestant churches support ministry through offerings, church tax or tithes.

sources.title: The Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles)
sources.author: Early Christian text, late first or early second century · New Advent edition
sources.shows: A travelling apostle should “take nothing but bread … but if he ask money, he is a false prophet”; yet “every true prophet that wills to abide among you is worthy of his support. So also a true teacher is himself worthy, as the workman, of his support.”
sources.application: The early church supported its teachers and distrusted those who asked for money: both at once.
sources.limits: An early church manual; its dating and setting are debated.

sources.title: Pricing
sources.author: Anthropic
sources.shows: Claude Sonnet 5.5 costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens; Claude Haiku 5.5 costs $0.10 and $0.50 for prompts up to 100,000 tokens.
sources.application: Every AI answer has a cost; the choice of model changes it many times over.
sources.limits: One provider’s list prices in US dollars; prices change, and other providers differ.

sources.title: ESV API: introduction
sources.author: Crossway
sources.shows: The text is free “for non-commercial use”; a commercial site “is primarily designed to motivate visitors to buy something, to pay for a service, or to give a donation, or it accepts advertising or sponsorships”. Other uses need permission.
sources.application: The translation an app uses can decide whether it may charge or ask for donations at all.
sources.limits: One publisher’s terms; others differ, and the Berean Standard Bible is in the public domain.

sources.title: With 330 million downloads, top Bible app celebrates 10 years
sources.author: Religion News Service · Word&Way, 27 July 2018
sources.shows: “An $8.3 million annual budget, funded by Life Church members’ tithes and outside donations, pays for YouVersion”; the app is “free with no commercial advertisements”.
sources.application: A free app is still paid for, here by a church and its donors.
sources.limits: A 2018 report; the current budget is not public in this source.

sources.title: TelefonSeelsorge
sources.author: TelefonSeelsorge Deutschland (Protestant and Catholic churches)
sources.shows: “Tag und Nacht erreichbar 0800 1110111 / 0800 1110222 oder 116 123”, by phone, chat or email.
sources.application: A first screen can carry a way to a person, day and night, free of charge.
sources.limits: Germany; other countries have their own services.

sources.title: To grow up healthy, children need to sit less and play more
sources.author: World Health Organization · 24 April 2019
sources.shows: For 1-year-olds, sedentary screen time “is not recommended”; for 2-year-olds it “should be no more than 1 hour; less is better”; “When sedentary, engaging in reading and storytelling with a caregiver is encouraged.”
sources.application: For young children, design for a grown-up reading and talking with the child, not for time alone with a screen.
sources.limits: Guidelines for children under 5, about physical activity, sitting and sleep.

sources.title: The New Coviewing: designing for learning through joint media engagement
sources.author: Joan Ganz Cooney Center at Sesame Workshop · 14 February 2012
sources.shows: A panel on how young children and “their influencers, from siblings to caregivers to teachers, can view media together”, framed by the report The New Coviewing (Takeuchi and Stevens, 2011). A producer warned that “children may be viewing by themselves” and urged “caution regarding the introduction of material that might be scary or isolating for a child”.
sources.application: Design for watching together, and take care with frightening material a child may meet alone.
sources.limits: A blog report of a panel discussion, not a study.

sources.title: Godly Play
sources.author: Wikipedia, on the method developed by Jerome Berryman
sources.shows: Lessons “are taught as stories, illustrated with hands-on materials, which are followed by ‘I wonder’ questions, then by time for students to creatively respond.”
sources.application: Open questions after a story let children make meaning and ask about what troubles them, without a right answer to find.
sources.limits: An encyclopedia summary; Berryman’s own guides are the primary source.

sources.title: App Store Review Guidelines: 1.3 Kids Category
sources.author: Apple
sources.shows: Kids Category apps “must not include links out of the app, purchasing opportunities, or other distractions to kids unless reserved for a designated area behind a parental gate”, and “should not include third-party analytics or third-party advertising.”
sources.application: A parental gate, and no third-party analytics or ads, are the baseline for a children’s app.
sources.limits: Applies to apps in Apple’s Kids Category; other children’s apps are not bound by it.

sources.title: Commission publishes guidelines on the protection of minors
sources.author: European Commission · 14 July 2025
sources.shows: Recommends “Setting minors’ accounts to private by default” and “Disabling by default features that contribute to excessive use, like communication “streaks,” ephemeral content, “read receipts,” autoplay, or push notifications”, removing persuasive design aimed at engagement and “putting safeguards around AI chatbots”.
sources.application: Private by default, no streaks or autoplay, and safeguards around chatbots, for any platform children can reach.
sources.limits: Guidelines under the Digital Services Act for online platforms; small and micro enterprises are exempt.

sources.title: Age appropriate design: a code of practice for online services
sources.author: Information Commissioner’s Office (UK)
sources.shows: Fifteen standards, beginning with “Best interests of the child” and including default settings, data minimisation, data sharing and geolocation.
sources.application: Make the child’s best interests the first test, with high-privacy defaults.
sources.limits: UK law for services likely to be accessed by children.

sources.title: FTC publishes updates to COPPA Rule
sources.author: Latham & Watkins · May 2025
sources.shows: The amended Children’s Online Privacy Protection Rule requires separate parental consent before children’s personal information is disclosed to third parties for purposes not integral to the service, a written data retention policy, and compliance by 22 April 2026.
sources.application: Ask parents separately before sharing anything about a child, and keep it only as long as needed.
sources.limits: A law firm’s summary of the US rule; the Federal Register text is authoritative.

sources.title: Bible App for Kids (App Store listing)
sources.author: Life.Church with OneHope · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: Free, rated 4+, with 9.4K ratings averaging 4.7. Its privacy label lists contact info (email address) under “Developer’s Advertising or Marketing”, with a note that practices “may vary … based on the features you use or your age.”
sources.application: A free children’s Bible app without ads can still collect a grown-up’s email for marketing; say whose data it is and why.
sources.limits: A store listing and self-reported label, not a test of the app; screens to be captured.

sources.title: Superbook Kids Bible (App Store listing)
sources.author: The Christian Broadcasting Network · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: “Videos, games, audio & more”: free, rated 4+, with 18K ratings averaging 4.8; its privacy label lists purchase history under “Developer’s Advertising or Marketing”.
sources.application: Games and episodes draw children in; check what the app collects and how it asks for purchases.
sources.limits: A store listing and self-reported label; screens to be captured.

sources.title: KonApp – Die App für Konfis (App Store listing)
sources.author: Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft · Apple App Store (Germany)
sources.shows: A group app for confirmation classes: “Man muss keine Daten von sich angeben, um teilzunehmen. Geteilte Daten werden sicher gespeichert und zuverlässig gelöscht.” Rated 4+, with 119 ratings averaging 2.9.
sources.application: A church-run youth app can ask for no personal details and delete what is shared.
sources.limits: A store listing; screens to be captured with a test group.

sources.title: 50.000 aktive Nutzer – Konfirmanden-App bleibt kostenlos
sources.author: epd · evangelisch.de, 12 March 2021
sources.shows: The KonApp, used by “50.000 jungen Leuten”, is to stay free; “Rund 4.500 Kirchengemeinden und andere Institutionen” had set up digital confirmation groups. It offers a group feed, a diary and materials.
sources.application: Churches can fund a free youth app with no advertising.
sources.limits: A 2021 news report; current figures may differ.

sources.title: Vereinbarung gemäß § 29 DSG-EKD (KonApp)
sources.author: Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft and each parish or institution · version of 11 August 2022
sources.shows: A joint-controller agreement under the EKD data protection law: the parish or institution obtains consent and can delete posts, participants and groups; nickname and profile photo are stored on the server; and “6 Wochen nach dem Konfirmationsdatum wird die Gruppe gelöscht”, unless an administrator switches this off.
sources.application: A church youth app can set out who is responsible for what, collect consent locally, and delete a group when the course ends.
sources.limits: A contract template from 2022; the current version may differ.

sources.title: Nummer gegen Kummer: Kinder- und Jugendtelefon
sources.author: Nummer gegen Kummer e.V.
sources.shows: “Ruf uns an unter 116 111”, “Montags bis samstags von 14-20 Uhr”; free and anonymous.
sources.application: A children’s helpline gives a child someone to talk to who is not part of their family or church.
sources.limits: Germany; other countries have their own children’s lines.

sources.title: AI Jesus – Bible Chat (App Store listing)
sources.author: Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: “Daily verse, Ask from GPT”, with “Unlimited chat with AI Jesus” about “relationships, faith, prayer, Life challenges”; Age Rating “4+”.
sources.application: An age rating says the content is not objectionable, not that the app was designed for children or has any safeguards for them.
sources.limits: One listing among many similar apps; the app was not tested.

sources.title: Human Interface Guidelines: Managing notifications
sources.author: Apple
sources.shows: Four interruption levels (Passive, Active, Time Sensitive, Critical); “Build trust by accurately representing the urgency of each notification.” “Never use the Time Sensitive interruption level to send a marketing notification.” “Make sure people can manage their notification settings within your app.”
sources.application: Mark reminders and daily content as ordinary or passive, never Time Sensitive, and give people their settings inside the app.
sources.limits: Platform guidance for Apple devices.

sources.title: App Store Review Guidelines: 4.5.4 Push Notifications
sources.author: Apple
sources.shows: “Push Notifications must not be required for the app to function”; promotions and direct marketing only if “customers have explicitly opted in to receive them via consent language displayed in your app’s UI”, with a way to opt out.
sources.application: Keep marketing out of reminders unless people asked for it separately.
sources.limits: Applies to apps on Apple’s App Store.

sources.title: Notification runtime permission
sources.author: Android Developers
sources.shows: “Before you ask users to grant any permissions, let them familiarize themselves with your app.” Good moments include when “The user taps an "alert bell" button.”
sources.application: Ask for notifications when someone sets a reminder.
sources.limits: Platform guidance for Android 13 and later.

sources.title: Batching smartphone notifications can improve well-being
sources.author: Nicholas Fitz, Kostadin Kushlev, Ranjan Jagannathan, Terrel Lewis, Devang Paliwal and Dan Ariely · Computers in Human Behavior, 2019
sources.shows: In a randomized field experiment (n = 237), participants whose notifications were “batched three-times-a-day felt more attentive, productive, in a better mood, and in greater control of their phones”; those with no notifications “experienced higher levels of anxiety and “fear of missing out” (FoMO)”.
sources.application: Fewer, predictable interruptions may serve people better than either constant alerts or none at all.
sources.limits: One study, self-reported outcomes over a short period; general phone notifications, not faith apps.

sources.title: A Sleeping, Recovering Bandit Algorithm for Optimizing Recurring Notifications
sources.author: Kevin P. Yancey and Burr Settles, Duolingo · KDD 2020
sources.shows: An algorithm to “optimize millions of daily reminders” led “to a 0.5 % increase in total daily active users (DAUs) and a 2 % increase in new user retention over a strong baseline.”
sources.application: Reminder wording and timing can be tuned for return; decide what a faith app should optimise, if anything.
sources.limits: A language-learning app; the measure is use, not benefit to the person.

sources.title: Emotional Manipulation by AI Companions
sources.author: Julian De Freitas, Zeliha Oğuz-Uğuralp and Ahmet Kaan-Uğuralp · Harvard Business School working paper, 2025
sources.shows: Analysing “1,200 real farewells”, companion apps “deploy one of six recurring tactics in 37% of farewells (e.g., guilt appeals, fear-of-missing-out hooks, metaphorical restraint)”; in experiments with 3,300 US adults, “manipulative farewells boost post-goodbye engagement by up to 14×”, driven by “reactance-based anger and curiosity—rather than enjoyment”.
sources.application: A persona that pleads, guilts or teases to keep someone is manipulating them; leave it out.
sources.limits: Replies to goodbyes in chat, not push notifications; general companion apps, not faith apps.

sources.title: Angelus
sources.author: Herbert Thurston · Catholic Encyclopedia (1907), Catholic Answers edition
sources.shows: The Angelus is “repeated three times each day, morning, noon, and evening, at the sound of the bell.” Its “history … is by no means easy to trace with confidence”, but “it is certain that the Angelus at midday and in the morning were of later introduction than the evening Angelus.”
sources.application: The church has long called people to prayer at shared hours with a bell.
sources.limits: A 1907 encyclopedia article; later scholarship refines its dates.

sources.title: St. Benedict’s Rule for Monasteries, chapters 16, 42, 43 and 47
sources.author: Benedict of Nursia, sixth century · Project Gutenberg edition
sources.shows: “Seven times in the day” (chapter 16); “Monks ought to be zealous for silence at all times, but especially during the hours of the night” (42); “as soon as the signal is heard, let them abandon whatever they may have in hand” (43); the signal “by day and by night shall devolve upon the Abbot” (47).
sources.application: The call to prayer is a responsibility of whoever gives it, kept to the hours, with silence at night.
sources.limits: A monastic rule; an app is not a monastery, and the analogy is ours.

sources.title: Bible Widgets: Verses & Prayer (App Store listing)
sources.author: Monkey Taps · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: Verses on the home and lock screens, “turning every phone unlock into a moment of connection with God”, with “Daily Reminders and Notifications”; 118K ratings, chart position #8 in Reference.
sources.application: A widget offers Scripture without interrupting; a reminder layer can still be added on top.
sources.limits: A store listing, not a test of the app.

sources.title: Blessed – Daily Verse & Prayer (App Store listing)
sources.author: Everblessed Technology · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: “a fresh evening Scripture and prayer prompt to quiet your mind, restore your heart, and remind you of God’s presence — even in the dark”, and “Get daily reminders, track your prayer streak”; 104K ratings.
sources.application: A daily word can be gentle, and the same app can count a streak.
sources.limits: A store listing, not a test of the app.

sources.title: Echo Prayer (App Store listing)
sources.author: The Parable Group · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: “After praying for someone, send out a notification to let them know you’ve prayed for their shared prayer”; reminders by push or email; 22K ratings.
sources.application: A notification can carry something a person did for someone else.
sources.limits: A store listing, not a test of the app.

sources.title: Intercede – Catholic Novenas (App Store listing)
sources.author: Devoted Coders · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: “timely, gentle reminders that ensure you never miss a day of your novena prayers”; 36K ratings.
sources.application: Reminders can follow the shape of a practice, such as the nine days of a novena, and end with it.
sources.limits: A store listing, not a test of the app.

sources.title: Universalis (App Store listing)
sources.author: Universalis Publishing · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: The Liturgy of the Hours and the Mass for every day, with “Home Screen widgets; liturgical events for your iOS calendar; daily email service … reminders and alarms”; 9.6K ratings, $9.99.
sources.application: An app for the hours offers reminders and alarms as tools, not as a strategy.
sources.limits: A store listing, not a test of the app.

sources.title: Hallow: Prayer & Meditation (App Store listing)
sources.author: Hallow · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: Minute meditations including the “Angelus”, and the “Ability to set prayer reminders”; 379K ratings.
sources.application: The largest Catholic prayer app offers the Angelus as content and reminders as a setting.
sources.limits: A store listing, not a test of the app.

sources.title: Bible Chat: Daily Devotional (App Store listing)
sources.author: Book Vitals · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: “spiritual prompts, Christian calendar reminders”, a lock-screen verse widget and a “Send a Blessing Widget”; 365K ratings, chart position #1 in Reference.
sources.application: The leading AI Bible app reaches people through reminders and widgets as well as chat.
sources.limits: A store listing; its notifications are on the diary list.

sources.title: App Store Review Guidelines: 3.2.1 (vi) and (vii), 3.2.2 (iv)
sources.author: Apple
sources.shows: “Approved nonprofits may fundraise directly within their own apps or third-party apps, provided those fundraising campaigns … offer Apple Pay support”; they “must disclose how the funds will be used” and “ensure appropriate tax receipts are available to donors”. Others “may only collect funds outside of the app, such as via Safari or SMS”. A gift “connected to or associated at any point in time with receiving digital content or services must use in-app purchase”.
sources.application: On iPhone, a gift is either a gift to an approved nonprofit, with Apple Pay, or collected outside the app; a gift that unlocks content is a purchase.
sources.limits: Rules for one platform; they change, and approval as a nonprofit is a separate process.

sources.title: Payments policy (Google Play)
sources.author: Google Play Console Help
sources.shows: Google Play’s billing is not required where “payments include peer-to-peer payments, online auctions, and tax exempt donations”.
sources.application: On Android, donations to tax-exempt organisations can use the organisation’s own payment provider.
sources.limits: A summary page of a longer policy; the exemption depends on the organisation’s status.

sources.title: When Should the Ask Be a Nudge? The Effect of Default Amounts on Charitable Donations
sources.author: Indranil Goswami and Oleg Urminsky · Journal of Marketing Research, 2016
sources.shows: Finds “a scale-back effect, in which low defaults reduce average donation amounts”, “a lower-bar effect, in which defaulting a low amount increases donation rate”, and “a default-distraction effect, in which introducing any defaults reduces the effect of other cues such as positive charity information”.
sources.application: A suggested amount changes who gives and how much; an empty field leaves the decision to the giver.
sources.limits: Charity appeals, not church giving; effects vary with the amounts tested.

sources.title: Hey Look at Me: The Effect of Giving Circles on Giving
sources.author: Dean Karlan and Margaret A. McConnell · NBER working paper 17737, 2012
sources.shows: A field experiment with donors to a Yale University service club: “charitable gifts increase in response to the promise of public recognition primarily because of individuals’ desire to improve their social image”.
sources.application: Showing givers to others raises giving, and does so through the motive Jesus warned against.
sources.limits: One university club in the United States.

sources.title: 2026 Protestant Annual Church Giving Report
sources.author: Ministry Brands, 2026
sources.shows: Churches that offer digital giving “reported that 41% of their giving came from digital methods”; “Recurring giving accounted for 35% of the digital giving in 2025”.
sources.application: Much church giving is now digital, and a third of it is regular.
sources.limits: A survey of church leaders and data from one vendor’s customers in the United States; the vendor sells giving software.

sources.title: ECFA Standards for Fund Raising
sources.author: Evangelical Council for Financial Accountability · Christianity Today, May 1987
sources.shows: Representations “must be current, complete and accurate. References to past activities or events must be appropriately dated”; “Fund raising appeals must not create unrealistic donor expectations of what a donor’s gift will actually accomplish”.
sources.application: A figure about what a gift does needs a date, a source and an honest scope.
sources.limits: The 1987 published standards; ECFA’s current wording is longer, with the same principle.

sources.title: A Statement on the Prosperity Gospel
sources.author: Lausanne Theology Working Group, Africa chapter · 2008–2009, published January 2010
sources.shows: Defines prosperity teaching as obtaining health and wealth “through positive confessions of faith and the “sowing of seeds” through the faithful payments of tithes and offerings”, and lists among its effects “Replacing the traditional call to repentance and faith with a call to give money”.
