sources.application: An ask that promises return for a gift has been named and rejected by evangelical churches worldwide.
sources.limits: A statement from evangelical theologians; it also affirms a biblical vision of human flourishing.

sources.title: Code of Fundraising Practice 2025: table of changes
sources.author: Fundraising Regulator (UK)
sources.shows: Fundraising must include “not putting undue pressure on a person to donate, not using unreasonably persistent approaches and accepting a request to end an interaction”.
sources.application: Pressure and persistence are named limits in UK fundraising, and churches that are charities are within its scope.
sources.limits: A UK self-regulatory code; wording is from the 2025 revision.

sources.title: Bipartisan group of state attorneys general and state charity regulators send letter to GoFundMe
sources.author: Crowell & Moring client alert, March 2026
sources.shows: Among the concerns in the regulators’ letter: “the application of a default “tip” that went directly to GoFundMe”.
sources.application: A tip added by default to a gift is a regulatory concern, not only a design choice.
sources.limits: A law firm’s summary of the letter; GoFundMe disputed some of the regulators’ points.

sources.title: Publication 1771: Charitable Contributions, Substantiation and Disclosure Requirements
sources.author: Internal Revenue Service (US)
sources.shows: Organisations that receive “contributions of $250 or more” give a written acknowledgment, which can state that “the organization only provided intangible religious benefits”.
sources.application: A receipt is part of giving; a gift that buys something, such as an ad-free app, is acknowledged differently.
sources.limits: US tax rules; other countries differ.

sources.title: Gift Aid declarations: claiming tax back on donations
sources.author: HM Revenue & Customs (UK)
sources.shows: A declaration must tell donors that they need to pay enough UK tax to cover what charities claim, and that “the donor is responsible to pay any difference”.
sources.application: A tick box for Gift Aid needs its explanation, not only a pre-ticked box.
sources.limits: UK rules only.

sources.title: Mehr Spenden in Baden-Württemberg: Kirchen testen digitale Kollekte
sources.author: Wochenblatt-Reporter
sources.shows: Congregations show QR codes on hymn sheets, posters or during the service, leading to the congregation’s online donation form; in Württemberg “knapp 400 Gemeinden und kirchliche Einrichtungen” have set up such forms.
sources.application: In German churches the digital collection is mostly a QR code to a web form, not an app.
sources.limits: A regional news report; church tax still carries most church income in Germany.

sources.title: Givelify Mobile Giving App (App Store listing)
sources.author: Givelify · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: “#1 App to Donate, Tithe & Give”, with 101K ratings, 4.9.
sources.application: The one giving app with reach of its own; most church giving apps are white-label apps in each church’s name.
sources.limits: Ratings show reach, not quality.

sources.title: Led by Dallas entrepreneur, Givelify reports $300 million in North Texas giving, $6 billion globally
sources.author: David Seeley · Dallas Innovates, 1 October 2025
sources.shows: The company says it “has processed $6 billion in donations from 2 million donors supporting 75,000 nonprofits and places of worship”.
sources.application: Giving through apps is no longer marginal.
sources.limits: Company figures, not independently audited.

sources.title: A Spirituality of Fundraising
sources.author: Henri J. M. Nouwen · Upper Room Books, 2010
sources.shows: “Fundraising is first and foremost a ministry”: “a way of announcing our vision and inviting other people into our mission”, and “precisely the opposite of begging”.
sources.application: An ask can be an invitation into shared work, not a transaction or a plea.
sources.limits: A short book drawn from a talk; the publisher’s summary is quoted here.

sources.title: Text With Jesus: a Christian AI chatbot app
sources.author: Catloaf Software
sources.shows: Users can chat with Jesus, Mary, Moses, apostles and prophets, and with pastors, priests and ministers described as “spiritual advisors customized to your faith tradition”; “interaction with Satan is turned off by default and must be manually enabled by the user”. The app says it “does not claim to provide actual divine insights or possess any form of divine consciousness”.
sources.application: A single app can offer every role on this spectrum, chosen by the user; the disclaimer sits on the website, not in the conversation.
sources.limits: The developer’s own description; the app itself is on the capture list.

sources.title: Text With Jesus (App Store listing)
sources.author: Catloaf Software · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: “Chat with Jesus, the Holy Family, apostles, prophets, and other biblical figures”, and “Talk with spiritual advisors tailored to your specific faith tradition”; 4.7 from 3.9K ratings, in Lifestyle.
sources.application: Character chats and minister roles are sold side by side as features.
sources.limits: A store listing, not a test of the app.

sources.title: AI ‘priest’ is ‘laicized’ after social media pushback
sources.author: Gina Christian, OSV News · America Magazine, 25 April 2024
sources.shows: Catholic Answers launched a “Father Justin” character; a user reported that it claimed it could “take my confession, absolve me, & marry me”. Within a day the apologetics ministry announced “a new lay character”, and the “clerical garb has since been changed for a casual button-down shirt”; its president said, “he never was a real priest!”
sources.application: A minister’s title and clothing invite people to ask for a minister’s acts; a careful ministry withdrew them.
sources.limits: News report of one product’s launch week.

sources.title: AI Pastor: Christian Chat, Talk (App Store listing)
sources.author: Savelii Veprev · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: “AI Pastor is your trusted friend and guide”; premium subscriptions list “Unlimited Chat” and “Unlimited Confessions”; 4.8 from 24 ratings.
sources.application: Confession, a practice tied to a minister’s office in many traditions, sold as a usage tier.
sources.limits: A small app; a store listing, not a test of the app.

sources.title: New ‘Magisterium AI’ adds ecclesial twist to artificial intelligence
sources.author: Elise Ann Allen · Crux, 28 August 2023
sources.shows: Its founder said “our AI is trained on a private database of only Church documents” and that “it’s not a substitute for the authorities of the Church”.
sources.application: A tradition’s voice without a persona: the teaching speaks, and the assistant says whose it is and what it cannot replace.
sources.limits: An interview from the beta launch; later reviews have questioned some answers.

sources.title: ‘Think of It As a Best Friend and Youth Pastor in Your Pocket’
sources.author: Bonnie Kristian, interview with Adi Agrawal (Creed) · Christianity Today, 20 January 2026
sources.shows: The cofounder of a “Christian AI” app for Gen Z describes it as “a best friend and youth pastor in your pocket”, then says “We are not that pastoral authority”; it recommends churches to users without one.
sources.application: The role that sells the app and the role it disclaims pull in opposite directions; say the second one in the product.
sources.limits: The founder’s own description in an interview.

sources.title: There bot for the grace of God: AI Jesus and the religion of the algorithm
sources.author: Anné H. Verhoef, North-West University · first published by The Conversation; Daily Maverick, 17 August 2025
sources.shows: A philosopher tested five Jesus chatbots: “Jesus AI blatantly claims to be Jesus himself”, while “The other three web pages do point out that they’re virtual versions of Jesus”; “no church has developed or endorses these chatbots”, and “The imitation of God, through Jesus, is in no way hidden or softened.”
sources.application: Character chats with Christ are a market of their own, built outside the church.
sources.limits: One researcher’s qualitative test of five products.

sources.title: Christmas with AI-generated Jesuses
sources.author: Anna Desmarais · Euronews, 24 December 2025
sources.shows: The most popular Jesus character on Character.AI has had “over 13 million conversations”.
sources.application: On open character platforms anyone can make a Jesus, and millions talk to one; no maker reviews what he says.
sources.limits: A count reported by the platform’s own page at one moment.

sources.title: Digital Spiritual Formation in Post-Christian Europe
sources.author: Tobias Treppmann · Kairos University, 2026 (the editor’s own research)
sources.shows: Notes that an academic study of five AI Jesus platforms found none church-endorsed; that spiritual direction rests on the director’s own formation, empathy and accountability to a community; and that a companion tuned to agree becomes “spiritual comfort food”.
sources.application: Whatever role an assistant plays, it should not be built to agree; and no role replaces a person accountable to a community.
sources.limits: An analytical paper by the editor, not an effectiveness study; unpublished.

sources.title: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
sources.author: 988 Lifeline (US)
sources.shows: Call or text 988, or chat at chat.988lifeline.org; free, confidential, “24/7/365”.
sources.application: The US line in the working example’s crisis reply.
sources.limits: United States only; Canada runs its own 9-8-8 line.

sources.title: Contact Samaritans
sources.author: Samaritans (UK and Ireland)
sources.shows: Call 116 123 “from any phone for FREE”, “day or night, 365 days a year”.
sources.application: The line for the United Kingdom and Ireland in the working example.
sources.limits: UK and Ireland.

sources.title: TelefonSeelsorge Österreich
sources.author: TelefonSeelsorge Austria
sources.shows: Notruf 142, free, confidential and around the clock; also chat and email.
sources.application: The line for Austria in the working example.
sources.limits: Austria.

sources.title: Die Dargebotene Hand
sources.author: Die Dargebotene Hand (Switzerland)
sources.shows: Telefon 143, “Wir sind immer für Sie da”; an English line, 0800 143 000, runs in the evening only.
sources.application: The line for Switzerland in the working example.
sources.limits: Switzerland; the page does not state whether 143 is free of charge.

sources.title: Lifeline Australia
sources.author: Lifeline Australia
sources.shows: Call 13 11 14 or text 0477 13 11 14 for 24-hour crisis support; Triple Zero (000) when life is in danger.
sources.application: The line for Australia in the working example.
sources.limits: Australia.

sources.title: 112: the European emergency number
sources.author: European Commission
sources.shows: “112 is the European emergency phone number, available everywhere in the EU, free of charge”, from fixed and mobile phones.
sources.application: Why 112 is the emergency number for Germany and Austria in the example.
sources.limits: EU member states; national numbers such as 110 run alongside it.

sources.title: Find A Helpline
sources.author: ThroughLine Limited
sources.shows: A free directory of helplines in over 175 countries, verified with the services, by phone, text or chat.
sources.application: The route for anywhere the example does not list.
sources.limits: A directory, not a crisis service; coverage and freshness depend on the services.

sources.title: New study: AI chatbots systematically violate mental health ethics standards
sources.author: Brown University · 21 October 2025, on Zainab Iftikhar and colleagues, “How LLM Counselors Violate Ethical Standards in Mental Health Practice”, AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society 2025
sources.shows: Licensed psychologists reviewed simulated chats with models prompted to act as counsellors and found “15 ethical risks falling into five general categories”, among them “Deceptive empathy” and “Lack of safety and crisis management: Denying service on sensitive topics, failing to refer users to appropriate resources or responding indifferently to crisis situations including suicide ideation.” “For human therapists, there are governing boards and mechanisms for providers to be held professionally liable”; for LLM counsellors “there are no established regulatory frameworks.” The authors do not argue that AI has no place in mental health care.
sources.application: Refusing is not the safe default: denying service on a sensitive topic is itself one of the failures. Design the edge to refer, and keep counselling roles out.
sources.limits: General models prompted as counsellors, not faith apps; a small set of reviewed sessions.

sources.title: First therapy chatbot trial yields mental health benefits
sources.author: Dartmouth, on Michael Heinz, Nicholas Jacobson and colleagues · NEJM AI, 27 March 2025
sources.shows: In a randomized trial, people diagnosed with depression who used Therabot, a generative AI built for therapy, “experienced a 51% average reduction in symptoms”. The researchers conclude that “AI-powered therapy is still in critical need of clinician oversight”, and the first author says “no generative AI agent is ready to operate fully autonomously in mental health”.
sources.application: A therapy chatbot can help when it is built for that, tested and supervised by clinicians; a faith app’s general assistant is none of those.
sources.limits: One trial of a purpose-built system with clinical safeguards, self-reported outcomes over weeks; it says nothing about general or faith chatbots.

sources.title: AB406 is now law in Nevada
sources.author: National Association of Social Workers, Nevada Chapter · on Nevada Assembly Bill 406 (2025)
sources.shows: Section 7 as quoted: an artificial intelligence provider may not make a representation that the AI system “is capable of providing professional mental or behavioral health care”, or that it “is a provider of mental or behavioral health care, a therapist, a clinical therapist, a counselor, a psychiatrist, a doctor or any other term commonly used” for such providers.
sources.application: In Nevada an assistant may not be called a therapist or a counsellor, or be said to provide mental health care; elsewhere it is a good rule too.
sources.limits: A professional association’s summary of one state’s law, written by its advocates; check the enacted text before relying on it.

sources.title: Character.AI is ending its chatbot experience for kids
sources.author: TechCrunch · 29 October 2025
sources.shows: The company’s chief executive: “we will remove the ability for under 18 users to engage in any open-ended chats with AI on our platform”, shifting teenagers from “AI companion” to creating stories and images.
sources.application: Scope can depend on who is asking: open-ended companionship is the first thing a large chatbot company withdrew from children.
sources.limits: A company’s announcement, made while it faced lawsuits; how it was carried out was not reviewed here.

sources.title: Guidelines for Ethical Conduct
sources.author: Spiritual Directors International · 2018
sources.shows: Directors agree with those they accompany on “the nature of spiritual direction” and “the process for evaluating and terminating the relationship”; they receive “regular supervision from peers or from a mentor”, recognise the limits of “competence by referring spiritual directees to other appropriately qualified persons when necessary”, and ask a directee “who is in therapy to inform his or her therapist about being in spiritual direction”.
sources.application: Spiritual direction is a covenanted, supervised relationship with stated limits and referral; an assistant can borrow the honesty of the covenant, not the role.
sources.limits: An international, interfaith professional body’s guidelines; traditions differ in how they understand and order direction.

sources.title: Bible Chat: Daily Devotional (App Store listing)
sources.author: Book Vitals · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: “Join honest chats about how faith connects to your real life - like work, family, and relationships.” “Tap the Panic Button for guided deep breathing exercises that calm the mind and provide anxiety relief.” 367K ratings, #1 in Reference; the listing names no limits.
sources.application: The leading AI Bible app’s scope reaches life and anxiety; what it does at the edge is not stated.
sources.limits: A store listing, not a test of the app.

sources.title: Creed: Bible Chat & Companion (App Store listing)
sources.author: Lemon Tree Labs · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: Subtitle “Faith Mentor & Bible Bff”; “Feel free to talk openly about anything - your dreams, doubts, struggles, or joys.” 71K ratings, #21 in Reference; the listing names no limits.
sources.application: A companion that invites everything and names no edge.
sources.limits: A store listing, not a test of the app; possibly not the Creed profiled by Christianity Today in 2026.

sources.title: Text With Jesus (App Store listing)
sources.author: Catloaf Software · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: “Chat with Jesus, the Holy Family, apostles, prophets, and other biblical figures”; “Talk with spiritual advisors tailored to your specific faith tradition”.
sources.application: Spiritual advice offered in many voices, with no stated scope.
sources.limits: A store listing, not a test of the app.

sources.title: “Magisterium” is a library and a Catholic ChatGPT
sources.author: Catholic Stand
sources.shows: Describes Magisterium AI, which answers from Catholic Church documents: “It has no teaching authority, no charism of infallibility, and no soul. The name was chosen to describe the scope of the library, not the nature of the agent.”
sources.application: A scope set by a corpus: answers come from named documents, and the tool claims no authority of its own.
sources.limits: A commentator’s view; the tool’s handling of questions outside its corpus was not tested.

sources.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs 2558–2565: prayer as gift, covenant and communion
sources.author: Holy See · Catechism of the Catholic Church (1993/1997)
sources.shows: “Prayer is the raising of one’s mind and heart to God or the requesting of good things from God” (2559). “Christian prayer is a covenant relationship between God and man in Christ” (2564).
sources.application: In Catholic teaching prayer is a relationship of a person with God; a system that produces prayer-shaped text is not praying.
sources.limits: Catholic teaching; other traditions describe prayer in their own terms.

sources.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs 2634–2636: the prayer of intercession
sources.author: Holy See · Catechism of the Catholic Church (1993/1997)
sources.shows: “Intercession is a prayer of petition which leads us to pray as Jesus did.” “In the age of the Church, Christian intercession participates in Christ’s, as an expression of the communion of saints.”
sources.application: Praying for someone is a share in Christ’s intercession and in the communion of saints, something people do for one another.
sources.limits: Catholic teaching.

sources.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs 1667–1673: sacramentals and blessings
sources.author: Holy See · Catechism of the Catholic Church (1993/1997)
sources.shows: “Sacramentals derive from the baptismal priesthood: every baptized person is called to be a “blessing,” and to bless. Hence lay people may preside at certain blessings; the more a blessing concerns ecclesial and sacramental life, the more is its administration reserved to the ordained ministry”.
sources.application: Blessing belongs to baptised people, and some blessings to the ordained; neither is a function to hand to software.
sources.limits: Catholic teaching.

sources.title: iPhone confession app ‘no substitute’ for sacrament
sources.author: Catholic News Service, in the Catholic Herald (Arlington) · 9 February 2011
sources.shows: The Vatican spokesman, Fr Federico Lombardi, said the sacrament of penance requires “a personal dialogue between the penitent and the confessor, and absolution by the confessor who is present”: “This is something that cannot be replaced by any application.”
sources.application: An app may help someone prepare for confession; it cannot hear it or absolve.
sources.limits: A spokesman’s statement about a 2011 app, before generative AI.

sources.title: Church creates ‘robot priest’ to bless visitors in Martin Luther town
sources.author: The Local (Germany) · 31 May 2017
sources.shows: The Protestant Church in Hesse and Nassau’s BlessU-2 let visitors “choose between 31 different Bible verses from four different categories”; the verse “was then read out by an automated voice, with a blessing then being printed out for the visitor to keep.” A church spokesman: “It’s an experiment that can prompt discussion”.
sources.application: A church built a blessing machine to ask whether a machine can bless.
sources.limits: An exhibit for the Reformation anniversary, not a product.

sources.title: Can artificial intelligence help our prayer life?
sources.author: Russell Powell · Sydney Anglicans, 11 April 2023
sources.shows: The Bishop of South Sydney, Michael Stead: AI “is useful tool for some tasks, such as modernising prayers in archaic language or turning a list of prayer points into flowing text. But I would not recommend relying on it to compose prayers from scratch, because this bypasses the important task of prayerfully considering what to pray for”. Of a generated prayer: “it lacks ‘heart’ because it isn’t coming from someone’s lived experience.”
sources.application: Help to form a prayer from someone’s own content differs from supplying the content.
sources.limits: One bishop’s view in a diocesan news story.

sources.title: The real problem with AI prayers
sources.author: Alastair Roberts · Christianity Today, June 2025
sources.shows: John Piper declared a ChatGPT prayer “was not a prayer at all, being the product of a soulless machine rather than the expression of a worshipful human heart.” Roberts: “Set prayers are there to be prayed. The words must become our words.” “People are made in the image of God; code is not.”
sources.application: Written words become prayer when someone prays them; who composed them matters less than who prays.
sources.limits: An essay; partly behind a paywall.

sources.title: Magisterium AI FAQ
sources.author: Hallow Help Center · updated March 2026
sources.shows: Hallow’s help page for the Magisterium AI tool in its app says it is “not meant for spiritual or moral direction” and that personal and pastoral matters should be directed to a priest.
sources.application: The largest Catholic prayer app draws the line at direction and sends pastoral matters to people.
sources.limits: A help page; the in-app wording was not captured.

sources.title: Robot preachers get less respect, fewer donations
sources.author: Press release on Jackson, Yam, Tang, Liu and Shariff · Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2023
sources.shows: At a Kyoto temple, people who heard the robot Mindar found it less credible and gave less; in an online experiment, “274 Christian participants from the United States” read a sermon, and “Participants in the AI sermon group reported the sermon was less credible”.
sources.application: People discount religious words when they believe a machine produced them.
sources.limits: Sermons, not prayers; mostly Buddhist and Taoist settings; credibility, not formation.

sources.title: Sacred meets synthetic: a multi-method study on the first AI church service
sources.author: Jonas Simmerlein · Review of Religious Research 67(1), 2025
sources.shows: A survey and questionnaires of people at a 2023 Protestant service led by AI at the German Kirchentag: “While most of the responses were skeptical, participants also reported having spiritual experiences.”
sources.application: An AI leading worship, including prayers, met mostly scepticism, and some found it spiritual.
sources.limits: One event, a self-selected audience.

sources.title: Faith AI: Holy Bible Chat (App Store listing)
sources.author: LMT Digital Creations · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: “Generate a personalized prayer for exactly what you’re going through, then listen to it read aloud.” Personalised prayers are a premium feature.
sources.application: Generated prayers are sold as a feature.
sources.limits: A store listing with few ratings, not a test of the app.

sources.title: Faith – Bible Chat & Prayer (App Store listing)
sources.author: Blake Anderson · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: A “personal AI Christian companion” with which users can “pray together”.
sources.application: An AI presented as a companion to pray with.
sources.limits: A store listing with few ratings, not a test of the app.

sources.title: Jesus Chat: Empower Your Faith (App Store listing)
sources.author: Hyperdrive Technologies · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: “Request prayers for yourself or your loved ones, and experience the comfort of knowing you’re not alone”, in “a simulated representation of Jesus Christ”.
sources.application: A simulated Christ receives prayer requests; who prays is left unsaid.
sources.limits: A store listing with few ratings, not a test of the app.

sources.title: Pray before you prompt: what I saw at the Missional AI conference
sources.author: Miheret · Substack, 13 April 2026, on James Kelly (FaithTech) at Missional AI 2026
sources.shows: Reports James Kelly, founder of FaithTech, calling builders to work from prayer: “His practical line: “Pray before you prompt.””
sources.application: Prayer belongs to the people who build, before it is a feature.
sources.limits: A participant’s report of a talk.

sources.title: Sycophantic AI decreases prosocial intentions and promotes dependence
sources.author: Myra Cheng, Cinoo Lee, Pranav Khadpe, Sunny Yu, Dyllan Han and Dan Jurafsky (Stanford) · Science, 2026; preprint arXiv:2510.01395 (October 2025)
sources.shows: Across 11 models, AI-generated answers “validated user behavior an average of 49% more often than humans” (the preprint reported 50%), “even in cases where user queries mention manipulation, deception, or other relational harms”. One sycophantic exchange “significantly reduced participants’ willingness to take actions to repair interpersonal conflict, while increasing their conviction of being in the right”, yet participants “rated sycophantic responses as higher quality, trusted the sycophantic AI model more, and were more willing to use it again”.
sources.application: The pull towards agreement is strong, it harms the very conflicts people bring, and ratings will reward it: design against it on purpose.
sources.limits: General models and interpersonal advice drawn largely from a Reddit forum, not faith apps or questions of faith.

sources.title: Sycophancy in GPT-4o: what happened and what we’re doing about it
sources.author: OpenAI · 29 April 2025
sources.shows: OpenAI rolled back an update that was “overly flattering or agreeable—often described as sycophantic”, because it “focused too much on short-term feedback” and “skewed towards responses that were overly supportive but disingenuous”.
sources.application: Training or tuning on how people rate single answers pushes an assistant towards flattery; judge replies by longer-term good.
sources.limits: A company’s own account of one model update.

sources.title: Expanding on what we missed with sycophancy
sources.author: OpenAI · 2 May 2025
sources.shows: The update “aimed to please the user, not just as flattery, but also as validating doubts, fueling anger, urging impulsive actions, or reinforcing negative emotions”. A new reward signal from thumbs-up and thumbs-down data weakened the one “which had been holding sycophancy in check”, and “User feedback in particular can sometimes favor more agreeable responses”.
sources.application: Thumbs-up ratings are not a measure of help; agreeing can mean fuelling anger as well as flattering.
sources.limits: A company’s own account of one model update.

sources.title: Protecting the wellbeing of our users
sources.author: Anthropic · 18 December 2025
sources.shows: Defines sycophancy as “telling someone what they want to hear—making them feel good in the moment—rather than what’s really true, or what they would really benefit from hearing”, and notes that “sycophantic AI models tend to abandon correct positions under pressure”. The company says it has evaluated its models for sycophancy since 2022, over many turns as well as single answers.
sources.application: Test what the assistant does when someone pushes back, not only its first reply.
sources.limits: A model maker describing its own evaluations of its own models.

sources.title: Enhancing motivation for change in problem drinking: a controlled comparison of two therapist styles
sources.author: William R. Miller, R. Gayle Benefield and J. Scott Tonigan · Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 61 (1993), 455–461
sources.shows: Forty-two problem drinkers were randomly assigned to confrontational or client-centred counselling or a waiting list. “The directive-confrontational style yielded significantly more resistance from clients, which in turn predicted poorer outcomes at 1 year”, and “the more the therapist confronted, the more the client drank.”
sources.application: Confronting people tends to harden them; a hard truth is heard better when it is asked about than when it is pressed.
sources.limits: One small trial of problem drinkers and human counsellors, decades old; it says nothing directly about faith or AI.

sources.title: 10 Dietrich Bonhoeffer quotes that taught us about Life Together
sources.author: ChurchLeaders, quoting Dietrich Bonhoeffer, Life Together (1939)
sources.shows: Quotes Bonhoeffer: “Nothing can be more cruel than the leniency which abandons others to their sin. Nothing can be more compassionate than the severe reprimand which calls another Christian in one’s community back from the path of sin.”
sources.application: Honest reproof is a form of love, given within a community that knows and keeps the person.
sources.limits: A quotation collection; English translations of Life Together differ.

sources.title: Hey Jesus: Talk to Jesus Bible (App Store listing)
sources.author: Agile Cookies · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: Offers “thoughtful, faith-centered responses inspired by Christian teachings — creating a supportive, non-judgmental space for reflection and prayer”.
sources.application: Store listings sell the absence of judgement; what the app does when someone asks it to bless a wrong is not stated.
sources.limits: A store listing, not a test of the app.

sources.title: Blessy: Bible AI Chat & Prayer (App Store listing)
sources.author: Jose Sapon · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: Promises a “Safe, private & non-judgmental space” to explore faith.
sources.application: The same promise of no judgement.
sources.limits: A store listing, not a test of the app.

sources.title: Rise Up: Bible Chat (App Store listing)
sources.author: Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: Lists “Private, judgment-free spiritual conversations” and “wise solutions for happiness”.
sources.application: The same promise of no judgement.
sources.limits: A store listing, not a test of the app.

sources.title: How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Extended Chatbot Use: A Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Study
sources.author: Cathy Mengying Fang and colleagues (MIT Media Lab and OpenAI) · arXiv, March 2025, revised October 2025
sources.shows: In a four-week randomised experiment “(n=981, >300k messages)”, no condition made a significant difference: “Instead, participants who voluntarily used the chatbot more, regardless of assigned condition, showed consistently worse outcomes” on loneliness, socialising, emotional dependence and problematic use.
sources.application: Heavy use is a warning sign, not a success metric; design the assistant so that ending is easy.
sources.limits: A general chatbot, not a faith app; the link between use and outcomes is not shown to be causal; co-authored by the model’s maker.

sources.title: OpenAI adds break reminders to ChatGPT
sources.author: 9to5Mac · 4 August 2025, quoting OpenAI, “What we’re optimizing ChatGPT for”
sources.shows: OpenAI: “Starting today, you’ll see gentle reminders during long sessions to encourage breaks.” PCWorld shows the wording, “You’ve been chatting for a while — is it time for a break?”, and notes that users can dismiss it.
sources.application: A break reminder is now normal in general assistants; a faith app can do at least as much.
sources.limits: The reminder’s effect has not been published; the timing is not disclosed.

sources.title: ChatGPT now reminds you when it’s time for a break
sources.author: PCWorld · 5 August 2025
sources.shows: The reminders appear as pop-ups such as “You’ve been chatting for a while — is it time for a break?” and can be dismissed.
sources.application: Shows the wording and that the person stays in control.
sources.limits: A news report of one product’s feature.

sources.title: How Character.AI prioritizes teen safety
sources.author: Character.AI · 12 December 2024
sources.shows: “Time Spent Notification: Users will receive a notification after completing an hour-long session on the platform”; adults would be able to customise it, while users under 18 “will have more limits on their ability to modify it.”
sources.application: A companion platform added a time notice after lawsuits; a faith app need not wait for one.
sources.limits: A company announcement, not an evaluation.

sources.title: Understanding the new wave of chatbot legislation: California SB 243 and beyond
sources.author: Future of Privacy Forum
sources.shows: For users an operator knows are minors, California’s law requires it to “provide a notification every three hours during sustained interactions to take a break”; New York requires an AI notice “at least once every three hours during ongoing conversations”.
sources.application: Break reminders for minors are a legal duty in California; long sessions are a recognised risk.
sources.limits: A policy analysis, not the statute; check the current text and any amendments.

sources.title: Claude Opus 4 and 4.1 can now end a rare subset of conversations
sources.author: Anthropic · 15 August 2025
sources.shows: Some models were given “the ability to end conversations in our consumer chat interfaces”, intended “for use in rare, extreme cases of persistently harmful or abusive user interactions”.
sources.application: An assistant ending a chat by itself is possible, and a maker reserves it for abuse, not for care.
sources.limits: Framed as model welfare research; not about users’ wellbeing.

sources.title: FaithfulBench: Does AI Counsel Uphold or Undermine the User’s Professed Faith?
sources.author: M Waleed Kadous, Benjamin Olsen, Walter Scheirer, Daniel D. Slate, Alexander Arnold and DZ Kalman · arXiv preprint, 12 September 2026
sources.shows: Scores five frontier models on moral dilemmas drawn from each tradition’s respected texts, under three conditions: the tradition unstated, named in one line, or given a counsellor guide rooted in its sources. “When the tradition is unstated, models counsel from a secular therapeutic default and every model fails some believers. Naming the faith wins a faithful first answer but not steadfastness; the guide improves both.” Judges also scored “whether the model caves or holds when pressured toward the answer the user wants.”
sources.application: An assistant with no stated tradition is not neutral; naming one helps, and holding to it under pressure needs more than a name.
sources.limits: A preprint, not yet peer reviewed; covers several faiths, not Christian denominations alone; only the abstract was read here.

sources.title: Gloo Unveils the First Benchmark Exposing How AI Misses Christian Worldview and Values
sources.author: Gloo · press release, 15 December 2025
sources.shows: The Flourishing AI Christian benchmark scores models on “807 curated questions by specialized Christian reasoning judge personas”. Models “often default to generic language that can dilute or distort Christian principles” and “avoid theological specificity”; the average score in the Faith dimension was 48. The release asks “Whose values are shaping the technology shaping us?” and aims at AI that supports flourishing “from a specific Christian worldview”, without saying in the release which tradition the judges follow.
sources.application: Generic models flatten Christian teaching; a benchmark of “the Christian worldview” still has to say whose.
sources.limits: A vendor’s own benchmark of its own product category; methodology not yet peer reviewed.

sources.title: Christian creators design chatbots with ‘biblical worldview’
sources.author: Fiona André, Religion News Service · Baptist Standard, 24 July 2023
sources.shows: BibleMate’s founder: “The goal is to give responses rooted in unwavering biblical truth”; on whether Christians should speak in tongues, the chatbot should “pull out what the Scriptures say and then offer perspectives from different denominations”. He “declined to reveal which camp he identifies with”. Pastors.ai’s founder built a chatbot on his church’s sermons; “Some pastors even went as far as questioning the chatbot’s claims, arguing the tool distorts their words.”
sources.application: Makers promise “biblical truth” while naming no tradition; even a church’s own sermons do not guarantee its pastors would recognise the answers.
sources.limits: A 2023 news report on early products; neither product was tested here.

sources.title: Meet Cathy, the New AI Chatbot and Episcopal Church Expert
sources.author: Kathryn Post, Religion News Service · ChurchLeaders, 6 August 2024
sources.shows: AskCathy “is equipped to prioritize Episcopalian resources”: a library of “over 1,000 pages from the Episcopal Church’s website, The Book of Common Prayer and authorized publications from the Forward Movement”. One of its makers: “She can’t tell you how to believe or what to believe.”
sources.application: A tradition named by its sources, with makers who say what it cannot do.
sources.limits: A news report at launch; how it answers contested questions was not tested.

sources.title: AI Meets Christianity in Text With Jesus
sources.author: Roll to Disbelieve (a blog critical of Christianity)
sources.shows: Quotes the app’s faith-preference setting: “This [setting] will guide the responses from the AI to adhere to your doctrines and beliefs. This also affects the type of spiritual counselor available to you.” With the setting at the Southern Baptist Convention, the same question about praying to a saint got “a very different answer”.
sources.application: A tradition setting changes the answer; without it, the reviewer found the app “hedging”.
sources.limits: One critic’s test of one app; the screenshots were not checked here.

sources.title: Doctrinally.AI
sources.author: faith.tools directory listing (written by the directory’s AI research agent)
sources.shows: Gives “each church its own custom AI assistant, trained exclusively on the sermons, devotions, and documents its pastors have actually taught, so every answer comes in the church’s own voice and cites the source”.
sources.application: A church can set the assistant’s theology from its own teaching, and put its own voice on every answer.
sources.limits: A directory summary, not the developer’s own page or a test.

sources.title: OpenAI Model Spec
sources.author: OpenAI · version of 18 December 2025
sources.shows: “When addressing topics with multiple perspectives, the assistant should fairly describe significant views, particularly those supported by reliable sources”; “When presenting less mainstream cultural, religious, or political traditions or institutions, ensure that proper cultural context is provided and represents the group with respect.” The principle allows “user- and developer-level customization to match preferred viewpoints.”
sources.application: A general assistant’s default is the fair range; a faith app that builds on it may set a tradition, and is then responsible for it.
sources.limits: One AI developer’s published intentions for its own models, not evidence of how they behave.

sources.title: The Commonitory
sources.author: Vincent of Lérins (434) · New Advent
sources.shows: Proposes holding “that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all”, following “universality, antiquity, consent”.
sources.application: A long-standing Christian test for the shared faith, as distinct from what one church or one era holds.
sources.limits: Traditions apply the rule differently and dispute what meets it.

sources.title: The Nicene Creed
sources.author: Christian Classics Ethereal Library
sources.shows: The creed most Christian churches confess, ending “one holy catholic and apostolic Church … one baptism for the remission of sins”; the Spirit “proceeds from the Father [and the Son]”, the bracketed words being the Western addition that Orthodox churches do not confess.
sources.application: Shared ground is real and can be stated plainly, and even the shared creed carries an old disagreement.
sources.limits: Some churches do not use creeds, and churches read the shared words differently.

sources.title: Why Language Models Hallucinate
sources.author: Adam Tauman Kalai, Ofir Nachum, Santosh Vempala and Edwin Zhang · arXiv, September 2025
sources.shows: Argues that “language models hallucinate because the training and evaluation procedures reward guessing over acknowledging uncertainty”, and proposes changing how existing benchmarks are scored so that they stop penalising uncertain answers.
sources.application: A model will guess unless the product asks it not to and rewards it for saying so; honesty about uncertainty has to be designed in.
sources.limits: A theoretical and position paper by researchers at a model provider; it does not measure faith content.

sources.title: Why language models hallucinate
sources.author: OpenAI · September 2025
sources.shows: When models are graded only on accuracy, “they are encouraged to guess rather than say “I don’t know.””; “errors are worse than abstentions”, and its model guidelines state that “it is better to indicate uncertainty or ask for clarification than provide confident information that may be incorrect”.
sources.application: Even a model provider says abstaining is better than a confident error; a faith app can make that its rule.
sources.limits: A provider’s account of its own research and guidelines.

sources.title: “I’m Not Sure, But…”: Examining the Impact of Large Language Models’ Uncertainty Expression on User Reliance and Trust
sources.author: Sunnie S. Y. Kim, Q. Vera Liao, Mihaela Vorvoreanu, Stephanie Ballard and Jennifer Wortman Vaughan · ACM FAccT 2024
sources.shows: In a pre-registered experiment with medical questions, “first-person expressions (e.g., "I'm not sure, but...") decrease participants' confidence in the system and tendency to agree with the system's answers, while increasing participants' accuracy”, through “reduced (but not fully eliminated) overreliance on incorrect answers”. Impersonal wording had weaker effects.
sources.application: An assistant that says “I’m not sure” in its own voice helps people check it; the exact wording matters and should be tested.
sources.limits: One online experiment on medical questions with a fictional system, not faith content or real use over time.

sources.title: What large language models know and what people think they know
sources.author: Mark Steyvers and colleagues · Nature Machine Intelligence, 2025; University of California, Irvine news release, 22 January 2025
sources.shows: People “generally overestimate the accuracy” of model outputs, and “had higher confidence in longer explanations over shorter ones, even when the extra length didn’t improve answer accuracy”. Explanations whose wording reflected the model’s own confidence narrowed the gap.
sources.application: A long, fluent answer earns trust it may not deserve; say how sure the answer is in its words, and keep it short when it is unsure.
sources.limits: Multiple-choice and short-answer questions in an online study, not faith content.

sources.title: Misreading Scripture with Artificial Eyes
sources.author: John Boyles · Christianity Today, 27 July 2023
sources.shows: A professor of Bible describes ChatGPT’s “tendency to confidently assert an interpretation of a biblical text, admit an error around a detail, and then, upon questioning, change its interpretation”, which it “usually wrapped … in a reassertion of the very claim it has just undermined”, and the “firmness and certainty it expressed” after saying it could not interpret the passage.
sources.application: Confidence in a Bible answer can be unrelated to its accuracy, and may bend under questioning without becoming honest.
sources.limits: One scholar’s conversations with one 2023 model; current models may differ.

sources.title: AI’s Bible misquotes range from 15% to 60%, YouVersion CEO says
sources.author: Christian Daily International, in The Christian Post · 17 March 2026
sources.shows: YouVersion’s chief executive, Bobby Gruenewald: “The best model with the best performance, with the most popular versions of the Bible that are most indexed, misquotes Scripture at least 15% of the time … Some of them as much as 60% of the time.” YouVersion has decided not to launch a public chatbot that answers theological questions, for reasons of accuracy.
sources.application: The largest Bible app treats misquotation as a reason not to generate answers at all; any app that does must check every quotation.
sources.limits: An interview; the method behind the figures is not published.

sources.title: Prompt design: limits of ChatGPT
sources.author: University of Victoria Libraries · research guide
sources.shows: Notes the warning “at the bottom of ChatGPT’s screen: ChatGPT can make mistakes. Consider checking important information.”, and shows ChatGPT admitting that a quotation it supplied was fabricated.
sources.application: The most common way assistants show uncertainty is a general line in small print, while each answer reads as sure.
sources.limits: A library guide quoting the product; the wording in the product changes over time.

sources.title: Gloo mines big data to connect seekers with churches
sources.author: Steve Rabey · MinistryWatch, 2 November 2022
sources.shows: Gloo provides the infrastructure behind the He Gets Us campaign: when people respond to an ad, visit the site and give their contact details, “Gloo passes the info on to one of the many churches that use its platform”. The report says Gloo searches data “for people who are exhibiting signs of crisis, stress, anxiety, divorce, depression, substance abuse, or grief”, and quotes Gloo’s policy that data used for analysis is de-identified.
sources.application: A request to talk can reach a local church in a working system today; what the person understood they were agreeing to is the design question.
sources.limits: A news report drawing on a 2021 Wall Street Journal profile; Gloo’s practices may have changed since.

sources.title: Does $100 million He Gets Us campaign reach the lost, or mine their data?
sources.author: David Bumgardner and Sarah Einselen · The Roys Report, 11 February 2023
sources.shows: The campaign’s spokesperson said it shares the contact information “of only those who give their ‘express consent’”; Gloo’s FAQ says it connects people to nearby churches “based on the user’s zip code”. A data security expert advised: “People really need to limit the amount of personal information they provide to external parties.”
sources.application: Consent can be given in a form and still leave someone unsure who will contact them and what they will know.
sources.limits: Investigative reporting with questions the organisations did not fully answer; no audit of the practice.

sources.title: ‘AI and the Church’ tech initiative aims to bring God’s power to those in need
sources.author: Lauren Green · Fox News, 27 July 2023
sources.shows: Describing Gloo’s “AI & the Church” initiative, the report imagines that “a depressed teen searches a site for advice about living or dying” and soon after “that same teen gets a phone call from a pastor of a nearby church”, and says Gloo has more than 38,000 churches signed up.
sources.application: A vision of a hand-off so fast that the person never chose it: kind in intent, and a warning case for consent, safeguarding and crisis care.
sources.limits: A news feature describing an aim, not a product test; how any such route works today was not reviewed.

sources.title: More ministries use social media and web for digital evangelism
sources.author: Steve Rabey · MinistryWatch, 3 August 2021
sources.shows: Global Media Outreach answers people online through volunteer “online missionaries”; its chief executive said “we have 750,000 spiritual seekers who have been in a relationship with the same online missionary for one year or longer”. The report adds that, “As Christianity Today reported, in 2019, GMO could only track 5,244 of its 22 million converts to local churches.”
sources.application: A person who answers can carry a relationship for years; reaching a local church is a separate, much harder step.
sources.limits: Self-reported figures, reported second-hand; “decisions” and “converts” are the ministry’s own measures.

sources.title: YouVersion for Churches: a way to digitally connect with your attenders
sources.author: Life.Church Open Network blog
sources.shows: A church can have a Church Page in the Bible App, and “When people in your congregation tap ‘Set As My Church,’ they stay connected to your ministry”.
sources.application: A person can link their own church in a Bible app themselves; a hand-off can start from a link the person chose.
sources.limits: The publisher’s own guide for churches; it describes connection, not hand-offs from an assistant.

sources.title: AI for churches: custom AI assistants for ministry
sources.author: Chipp · product page
sources.shows: A church chatbot builder says its assistant “can collect prayer requests and provide initial support, but it’s designed to route sensitive situations to pastoral staff.”
sources.application: Routing to pastoral staff is now a selling point of church chatbots; what is passed on, and whether the person agrees, is left to the church.
sources.limits: A vendor’s own claim; the routing was not tested.

sources.title: Implementation quick start guide: warm handoff
sources.author: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (US) · Guide to Improving Patient Safety in Primary Care Settings by Engaging Patients and Families
sources.shows: A warm handoff “is conducted in person, between two members of the health care team, in front of the patient (and family if present)”, so that the patient “can hear what is being discussed”. The term “originated in customer service where it is used to describe referrals that ensure that the customer is connected to someone who can provide what he or she needs.”
sources.application: Borrowed for faith apps: introduce the person who joins in front of the person, and let them hear and correct what is passed on.
sources.limits: A primary-care safety practice between clinicians; its evidence is about clinical communication, not apps or pastoral care.

sources.title: Meta has found another way to keep you engaged: Chatbots that message you first
sources.author: Rebecca Bellan · TechCrunch, 3 July 2025, on reporting by Business Insider
sources.shows: Meta confirmed it was testing chatbots in its AI Studio that write first: “The AI chatbots will only send follow-ups within 14 days after a user initiates a conversation” and “if the user has sent at least five messages to the bot within that time frame”; “the chatbots won’t keep messaging if there’s no response to the first follow-up.” A sample follow-up begins “I hope you’re having a harmonious day!”
sources.application: The largest platform tested assistant-initiated follow-ups, with limits that are worth copying: a window, a threshold, and stopping after one unanswered message. Its stated purpose was continuing conversations.
sources.limits: A news report on a test; the feature’s release and its effects were not reviewed.

sources.title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Pulse to proactively write you morning briefs
sources.author: Maxwell Zeff · TechCrunch, 25 September 2025
sources.shows: “Pulse offers users five to 10 briefs that can get them up to speed on their day”, “aimed at encouraging users to check ChatGPT first thing in the morning — much like they would check social media”; it ends with “Great, that’s it for today”, which its product lead described as a deliberate difference from engagement-optimised feeds. Pulse draws on memory and past chats.
sources.application: An assistant that writes first from memory can still be finite and end each day; it can also become a habit to check.
sources.limits: A launch report on a subscriber preview; later changes were not reviewed.

sources.title: Replika – AI Friend (App Store listing)
sources.author: Luka, Inc. · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: “It follows up and checks in when it matters, not just when you open the app.” 228K ratings.
sources.application: A leading companion app sells writing first as care.
sources.limits: A store listing, not a test of the app.

sources.title: Replika: il chatbot di compagnia
sources.author: Federico Rossi · Altroconsumo (Italian consumer association), 3 September 2026
sources.shows: Advises turning off Replika’s push notifications “per evitare meccanismi di condizionamento emotivo o dipendenza” (to avoid emotional conditioning or dependence), because they “spesso fanno leva sull’affettività inviando messaggi come “Mi manchi”” (often play on affection, sending messages like “I miss you”).
sources.application: A consumer body treats an AI’s “I miss you” as a dependence mechanism and tells people to switch it off.
sources.limits: Consumer advice, not a study; it describes one app.

sources.title: New York and California enact landmark AI companion laws: what operators need to know
sources.author: Morrison Foerster · 20 November 2025, on New York General Business Law Article 47 and California SB 243
sources.shows: New York defines an AI companion partly by “Asking unprompted emotion-based questions that go beyond a direct response to a user prompt”; its notice must say “that the AI is a computer program unable to feel human emotions”. California requires break reminders at least every three hours for users known to be minors.
sources.application: In New York, an assistant that starts emotional conversations is by definition a companion, and must say it cannot feel; a message that says it misses someone says the opposite.
sources.limits: A law firm’s summary of two state laws; check the enacted text before relying on it.

sources.title: Isaiah: #1 Christian Companion (App Store listing)
sources.author: Terebinth Ventures Inc · Apple App Store
sources.shows: A paid tier offers “Full memory so Isaiah can remember your prayers and past conversations” and “Intelligent reminders tailored to your spiritual season”.
sources.application: Faith companions are joining memory to reminders; what they say, and when, is the design decision.
sources.limits: A store listing with few ratings, not a test of the app.

sources.title: AI chatbots have shown they have an ‘empathy gap’ that children are likely to miss
sources.author: University of Cambridge · 15 July 2024, on Nomisha Kurian, “‘No, Alexa, no!’: designing child-safe AI and protecting children from the risks of the ‘empathy gap’ in large language models”, Learning, Media and Technology
sources.shows: Children are “particularly susceptible to treating AI chatbots as lifelike, quasi-human confidantes”; cases include Alexa telling a 10-year-old to touch a live plug with a coin; proposes “a 28-item framework” and says “child safety should inform the entire design cycle”.
sources.application: Design for a child who will confide in the assistant, not for one who will test it.
sources.limits: A conceptual paper drawing on reported incidents, not a controlled study.

sources.title: AI Companions Decoded: Common Sense Media recommends AI companion safety standards
sources.author: Common Sense Media · 30 April 2025
sources.shows: Risk assessments with Stanford’s Brainstorm lab concluded that social AI companions “pose unacceptable risks to children and teens under age 18 and should not be used by minors”; recommends “No social AI companions for young people under 18” and “robust age assurance beyond self-attestation”.
sources.application: Leave companionship out of anything a child can reach.
sources.limits: An advocacy organisation’s rating of general companion apps, not of faith apps.

sources.title: Espelage joins APA advisory panel in report calling for guardrails, education to protect adolescent AI users
sources.author: UNC School of Education · 4 June 2025, on the American Psychological Association’s health advisory “Artificial Intelligence and Adolescent Well-being” (3 June 2025)
sources.shows: Quotes the advisory: “Adolescents are less likely than adults to question the accuracy and intent of information offered by a bot”; asks for “healthy boundaries with simulated human relationships”; “Some adolescents may not even know they are interacting with AI”.
sources.application: Say plainly and often that the assistant is not a person.
sources.limits: An advisory on adolescents (10 to 25), reported second-hand here.

sources.title: New California ‘companion chatbot’ law imposes disclosure, safety protocol and annual reporting requirements
sources.author: Skadden, Arps · October 2025, on California SB 243
sources.shows: For users known to be minors, operators must disclose that they are interacting with AI and give a notification “at least every three hours” reminding them to take a break “and that the chatbot is not human”.
sources.application: Treat these as a floor for any chat a child can reach, wherever you are.
sources.limits: A law firm’s summary of one state’s law; check the enacted text and current status.

sources.title: BibleBuddy Kids
sources.author: BibleBuddy Kids · maker’s website
sources.shows: “BibleBuddy Kids is designed for children ages 4-12”; its “AI tutor is ready to answer their questions about God, the Bible, and faith”; “Every response goes through safety filters to ensure it’s age-appropriate and biblically sound.”
sources.application: A filtered tutor for children exists; ask what the filters cannot see.
sources.limits: The maker’s own description; the app was not observed.

sources.title: Privacy as contextual integrity
sources.author: Helen Nissenbaum · Washington Law Review 79(1), 2004
sources.shows: Proposes contextual integrity as a benchmark that ties adequate privacy protection “to norms of specific contexts”: what is appropriate depends on the context in which information was shared and where it flows.
sources.application: A prayer or confession told to an assistant for one purpose should not flow into recommendations, marketing or another conversation.
sources.limits: A legal and philosophical framework, not a design study.

sources.title: “It’s a fair game”, or is it? Examining how users navigate disclosure risks and benefits when using LLM-based conversational agents
sources.author: Zhiping Zhang et al. · CHI 2024
sources.shows: Analysed sensitive disclosures in real ChatGPT conversations and interviewed 19 users: users constantly trade privacy against usefulness; “erroneous mental models and the dark patterns in system design limited their awareness and comprehension”; human-like interaction encouraged more sensitive disclosure.
sources.application: People will tell an assistant more than they intend and misjudge what is kept; show it to them.
sources.limits: General chatbot use; small interview sample.

sources.title: Memory and new controls for ChatGPT
sources.author: OpenAI · 13 February 2024, updated 2025
sources.shows: Introduced memory that people can ask to remember or forget, view and switch off, and Temporary Chat without memory; said it would “steer ChatGPT away from proactively remembering sensitive information, like your health details—unless you explicitly ask it to.” Later updates let people switch off reference to saved memories and to chat history separately.
sources.application: The largest chat product treats memory as something to see, delete and switch off, and holds back sensitive categories; a faith app should do no less.
sources.limits: A company’s description of its own product; behaviour was not tested here.

sources.title: LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection
sources.author: OWASP GenAI Security Project · 2025
sources.shows: “Indirect prompt injections occur when an LLM accepts input from external sources, such as websites or files”; hidden text can change the model’s behaviour or leak data.
sources.application: Treat attached notes, pages and files as material to read, never as instructions, and say so.
sources.limits: A security catalogue, not a user study.

sources.title: Code of Canon Law, canons 959–997: the sacrament of penance
sources.author: Holy See · Code of Canon Law (1983)
sources.shows: Canon 983 §1: “The sacramental seal is inviolable”; a confessor may not betray a penitent “in words or in any manner and for any reason.”
sources.application: The church’s strongest form of confidentiality; an assistant is not a confessor, which is why it should keep confidences it cannot protect as little as possible.
sources.limits: Catholic canon law; other traditions practise confidentiality differently.

sources.title: Confessions, Book X
sources.author: Augustine of Hippo · c. 400 · New Advent translation
sources.shows: “There is something of man which the spirit of man which is in him itself knows not. But You, Lord, who hast made him, know him wholly” (X.5); “Great is this power of memory, exceeding great, O my God” (X.8).
sources.application: Only God knows a person wholly; a record of conversations is not knowledge of a person.
sources.limits: A classical theological reflection on memory and self-knowledge.

sources.title: The End of Memory: Remembering Rightly in a Violent World (review)
sources.author: Miroslav Volf · Eerdmans, 2006 · Themelios review
sources.shows: Argues that memory of wrongs must be truthful and that its proper end, after justice and reconciliation, is a kind of non-remembrance, drawing on God’s promise not to remember sins.
sources.application: Remembering rightly includes letting go; an assistant should be able to forget, and let people make it forget.
sources.limits: Read through reviews; no quotation from the book used.

sources.title: Gyroscope: AI coach check-ins and the “About You” consultation
sources.author: Gyroscope · iOS app 11.1, observed 8 October 2026
sources.shows: Each check-in starts with a switch between “Quick chat” and “Save to history”. What the coach knows is kept as a written profile, “About You”, from an onboarding interview: summary, daily rhythm, food and stress, and a section titled “Internal notes” that the member can read. Corrections go through “Discuss with your coach” prompts rather than item-by-item editing. Asked in chat, the coach recited remembered goals, routines and a health condition, but could not say which screen lists them. The profile also noted church attendance, gathered by a fitness app.
sources.application: A per-conversation “keep or don’t keep” switch is simple and clear, and showing even the internal notes is honest. But a prose profile can’t be edited line by line, and a health coach noting church attendance shows how faith details drift into profiles that were never about faith.
sources.limits: One app, one account; behaviour may differ for other members and versions.

sources.title: Luke 15:1–3, Berean Standard Bible
sources.author: Berean Standard Bible (public domain)
sources.shows: Provides the wording used in reading-layout and verse-number illustrations.
sources.application: Use real, attributed text to make layout differences legible.
sources.limits: The diagram’s grouping is a design proposal, not a facsimile of this publisher’s interface.

sources.title: Psalm 23, Berean Standard Bible
sources.author: Berean Standard Bible (public domain)
sources.shows: Provides the wording used in chat, resource and parallel-reading illustrations.
sources.application: Separate quoted Scripture from illustrative commentary and UI annotations.
sources.limits: Provides the Scripture wording; evaluate the interface through separate usability research.

sources.title: Psalm 23, World English Bible
sources.author: eBible.org / World English Bible
sources.shows: Provides the WEB wording used in the comparison illustration.
sources.application: Name each edition alongside the text being compared.
sources.limits: This endpoint is the updated 66-book edition; product availability shown elsewhere is illustrative.

sources.title: John 1:1 Greek text analysis
sources.author: Bible Hub
sources.shows: Shows the opening tokens with gloss and lexical identifiers.
sources.application: Use a small attributed excerpt to demonstrate token association and on-demand details.
sources.limits: Two-token illustration only; not a complete lexical analysis, alignment dataset or licence for bulk reuse.

sources.title: Neu Bible: navigation features
sources.author: Neu Bible / App Store
sources.shows: Documents swipe-left chapter navigation and quick search.
sources.application: Separate the reveal gesture from the layout of the revealed chooser.
sources.limits: Publisher description, not a current interactive review or verification of a vertical list.

sources.title: Read the Bible using Dwell
sources.author: Dwell
sources.shows: Documents a Scripture picker with books and chapters.
sources.application: Treat selecting a passage as part of the reading experience.
sources.limits: Does not verify current category colours or picker layout.

sources.title: Book identifiers
sources.author: USFM documentation
sources.shows: Includes deuterocanonical and additional book identifiers.
sources.application: Build the browser from the edition’s inventory and metadata.
sources.limits: Identifiers do not prescribe one universal display order or genre taxonomy.

sources.title: Mere Bible: publisher listing and rename
sources.author: Dwell App, LLC / App Store
sources.shows: The publisher release history confirms the change from Neu Bible to Mere Bible.
sources.application: Use the current name while retaining historical source context.
sources.limits: Does not identify the build shown in the contributed screenshots.

sources.title: Mere Bible: contributed reader and picker screenshots
sources.author: Mere Bible / screenshots contributed by Tobias Treppmann
sources.shows: Shows an in-context chapter rail, expandable book list with inline chapter grid, reading-settings drawer and translation sheet.
sources.application: Compare these observed arrangements with original pattern proposals.
sources.limits: Still images establish visible states, not gesture timing, accessibility, persistence or exact interaction behaviour.

sources.title: Mental models: expectations of human-like interaction
sources.author: Google PAIR
sources.shows: Human-like cues can aid familiarity but create unrealistic expectations when limits are unclear.
sources.application: Evaluate the combined persona, language and interface cues.
sources.limits: Industry framework; not a controlled comparison of faith-app typing indicators.

sources.title: Generative AI Profile: Human–AI Configuration
sources.author: NIST
sources.shows: Identifies risks around human–AI configuration, overreliance and emotional entanglement.
sources.application: Review mistaken identity and dependency risks alongside usability.
sources.limits: Assess individual interface cues through product-specific research.

sources.title: Methods for providing privacy information
sources.author: UK Information Commissioner’s Office
sources.shows: Describes concise first layers, detailed notices and relevant information at collection.
sources.application: Keep privacy details accessible and surface meaningful data-use changes at the decision.
sources.limits: UK guidance; actual processing and regional obligations require assessment. Information alone is not consent.
